{{Shrine |Name = Shiba Daijingu (芝大神宮) |image = [[File:Shiba-daijingu1.jpg|260px|Shiba Daijingu]]
Worship Hall
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=260|coord={{coord|35|39|27.5|N|139|45|11|E}}}} |Location = 1‑12‑7 Shiba Daimon, Minato, Tokyo {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Latitude = 35|Minutes = 39|Seconds = 27.5 |Longitude = 139|Minutes = 45|Seconds = 11 |Enshrined Deities = {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|12=draft}}
{{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|12=draft}} {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Shrine Rank = Former Prefectural Shrine · {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft}} · Tokyo Ten Shrines |Foundation = {{ill|1005|ja|1005|12=draft}} ({{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|12=draft}} 2) October 21 |Main Hall = Built in the Shinmei-zukuri style |Alternate Names = Shiba Jinmyōgū · Iikura Jinmyōgū · The Ise of Kanto |Annual Festival = September 16 {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Rituals = Hanchō Festival (February 3)
Dara Dara Festival (September 11–21)
Savings Festival (October 17) }} [[File:Shiba-daijingu 01.jpg|thumb|Worship Hall facing east]] '''Shiba Daijingu''' (芝大神宮) is a {{ill|Shinto Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in 1‑chome of {{ill|Shiba Daimon|ja|芝大門|12=draft}}, in {{ill|Minato|ja|港区 (東京都)|lt=Minato|lt_ja=港区|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|12=draft}}. At one time it was one of the {{ill|Tokyo Ten Shrines|ja|東京十社|12=draft}} designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank under the modern system being that of a {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|府県社|12=draft}}. == 社名 == Originally, the shrine was simply called “Shinmei” or “Shinmeigū.” Because it was once enshrined in Hibiya-gō in {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|12=draft}}, it came to be known as “Hibiya Shinmei (Hibiya Shinmeigū)”; and because it was later enshrined at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|12=draft}} (later known as Iikura Shō in Musashi Province), it was also called “Iikura Shinmei (Iikura Shinmeigū).” Furthermore, as residents settled in the Shiba area and the town took shape, the name “Shiba Shinmei (Shiba Shinmeigū)” was adopted.{{efn|In Bunsei 10 ({{ill|1827|ja|1827|12=draft}}), in the “Temple and Shrine Records” section of the “Document of Geographical Survey of Temples and Shrines” (文政寺社町方書上) compiled for the purpose of the “Gofunai Bikō” ({{ill|Gofunai Bikō|ja|御府内備考|12=draft}}) by the Bakufu ({{ill|Bakufu|ja|Tokugawa shogunate|lt=Bakufu|12=draft}}), the cover was inscribed “Shiba Shinmeisha,” while the document submitted by the shrine to the Bakufu called it “Iikura Shinmeigū.”}} In addition, because the deities of both the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft}} are enshrined here, the shrine played a central role in {{ill|Ise Worship|ja|伊勢信仰|12=draft}} in the Kantō region and was respectfully called “The Ise of Kanto.” With the advent of the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft}}, and with the approval of the government’s {{ill|Ministry of Religion|ja|教部省|12=draft}}, {{ill|Daijō-kan Shōin|ja|太政官正院|12=draft}} and {{ill|Tokyo Prefecture|ja|東京府|12=draft}}, from {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 5 ({{ill|August 30 (old calendar)|ja|8月30日 (旧暦)|lt=August 30|lt_ja=8月30日|12=draft}}) ({{ill|1872|ja|1872|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 2|ja|10月2日|12=draft}}) onward the present name “Shiba Daijingu” was adopted. == {{nihongo|Worshipped deities|祭神|Saijin}} == * {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|12=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮内宮|lt=Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=皇大神宮|12=draft}}. * {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|12=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮外宮|lt=Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=外宮|12=draft}}. Unusually for a Tokyo shrine, talismans of Toyouke Ōmikami are also issued. ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|lt_ja=源頼朝公|12=draft}} ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|lt_ja=徳川家康公|12=draft}} == History == It is said that the shrine traces its origins to a {{ill|Shinmei Shrine|ja|神明社|12=draft}} established at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|12=draft}} – the kitchen ({{ill|Gochū|ja|御厨|12=draft}}) of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft}} located in Musashi Province – as recorded in the work 『{{ill|Shinpōshō|ja|神鳳鈔|12=draft}}』. Initially the shrine was enshrined on Iikura-yama (now, {{ill|Shiba Park|ja|芝公園|12=draft}} in Minato). According to the shrine legend, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft}}, in {{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|12=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1005|ja|1005|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 21|ja|10月21日|12=draft}}) on {{ill|September 16 (old calendar)|ja|9月16日 (旧暦)|lt=September 16|lt_ja=9月16日|12=draft}}, the inner and outer shrines of Ise were enshrined ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}) and a stone known as “Utodoishi” and a sword—both regarded as sacred treasures—were offered. It is said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|12=draft}} twice donated shrine domain lands, in {{ill|Genryaku|ja|元暦|12=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1185|ja|1185|12=draft}}) and in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|1193|ja|1193|12=draft}}); in the latter instance, over 1,300 kan of land was donated as a shrine domain ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}). Later in the medieval period the shrine was held in high esteem by the warrior families of eastern Japan. In {{ill|Kenmu|ja|建武|12=draft}} 4 on {{ill|January 7 (old calendar)|ja|1月7日 (旧暦)|lt=January 7|lt_ja=1月7日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1337|ja|1337|12=draft}}, {{ill|February 8|ja|2月8日|12=draft}}), the younger brother of {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|ja|足利尊氏|12=draft}}, namely {{ill|Ashikaga Naoyoshi|ja|足利直義|lt=Ashikaga Naoyoshi|lt_ja=直義|12=draft}}, offered a letter of reward in recognition of prayers for military success (a document written by Naoyoshi that is preserved at the shrine). During the 【Sengoku period】, the shrine also received veneration from {{ill|Ota Dokan|ja|太田道灌|lt=Ota Dokan|lt_ja=太田資長（道灌）|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 16 on {{ill|July 24 (old calendar)|ja|7月24日 (旧暦)|lt=July 24|lt_ja=7月24日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1588|ja|1588|12=draft}}, {{ill|September 14|ja|9月14日|12=draft}})), an official edict concerning Shibamura was issued by {{ill|Hojo Ujinao|ja|北条氏直|lt=Hojo Ujinao|lt_ja=北条氏直|12=draft}} (this edict is also preserved at the shrine). Furthermore, around {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 18 on {{ill|July 19 (old calendar)|ja|7月19日 (旧暦)|lt=July 19|lt_ja=7月19日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1590|ja|1590|12=draft}}, {{ill|August 18|ja|8月18日|12=draft}})), {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft}} prayed for military victory when dispatching forces from Edo to pacify the Ou region, and in the same year, on {{ill|August 1 (old calendar)|ja|8月1日 (旧暦)|lt=August 1|lt_ja=8月1日|12=draft}} ({{ill|August 30|ja|8月30日|12=draft}}), {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft}} visited the shrine upon his entry into Edo; then, in the following year on {{ill|November 28 (old calendar)|ja|11月28日 (旧暦)|lt=November 28|lt_ja=11月28日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1592|ja|1592|12=draft}}, {{ill|January 12|ja|1月12日|12=draft}})), he donated 15 koku of land in Hibiya of Musashi Province as shrine domain. In {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長|12=draft}} 3 (1598) in August, when {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|12=draft}} was relocated from the shrine’s former site (Shiba Park), the shrine was moved to its present location (Shiba Daimon, Minato). In the 5th year ({{ill|1600|ja|1600|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 7|ja|10月7日|12=draft}}) following the move, Ieyasu himself visited the shrine on his way to the {{ill|Battle of Sekigahara|ja|関ヶ原の戦い|lt=Sekigahara|lt_ja=関ヶ原|12=draft}} to pray for victory; and during the Siege of Osaka in the 19th to 20th years, as a proxy for the shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|ja|徳川秀忠|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|lt_ja=秀忠|12=draft}}’s principal wife Oeyo ({{ill|Sūgen-in|ja|崇源院|12=draft}}), the nurse of {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|ja|徳川家光|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|lt_ja=家光|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kasuga no Tsubone|ja|春日局|12=draft}} made a shrine visit. Thereafter, under the patronage of successive shōguns and the Bakufu, the construction and repair of the shrine buildings were executed by imperial orders, and various prayer requests were received from the Bakufu (for example, a prayer for safe delivery on the occasion of the birth of the 4th shōgun, {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|12=draft}}) – and the shrine was also revered by feudal lords and other regional authorities (for instance, repairs to the shrine buildings were undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|12=draft}} of the Fukui Domain, and the lord of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|lt=Satsuma Domain Lord|lt_ja=薩摩藩主|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|12=draft}}, enshrined the deity in Kagoshima (presently at {{ill|Taga Shrine|ja|多賀神社 (鹿児島市)|lt=Taga Shrine|lt_ja=多賀神社|12=draft}} in Shimizu-cho, Kagoshima City)).{{efn|Examples include the safe-delivery prayer for the birth of the 4th shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|12=draft}}, and the shrine repairs undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|12=draft}} of the Echizen Fukui Domain, as well as the enshrinement by the lord of the Satsuma Domain, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|12=draft}}, in Kagoshima.}} {{efn|Regarding the above, the following is an excerpt from the “Bunsei Jūnen Shojō” (文政十年書上) that records the shrine’s founding legend for reference: {{Quotation| The origin of enshrining the twin deities at the Great Shrine in Hibiya-gō of Toyoshima District in Musashi Province is said to date from the sixteenth day of September in the second year of Kankō during the reign of Emperor Ichijō. On that day, a sacred token together with a large fang descended upon this place. All the village’s elders, youths, and children gathered, and though they were at first suspicious of the seemingly miraculous descent of this divine token of Shinmei, a little girl inexplicably approached. Her face changed as she hurriedly proclaimed, “I am the divine wind—the deity of both the inner and outer shrines of Ise—and because there is military strife in these eastern lands, I have come down to subdue the armies and mark this place as my dwelling.” Thus, two types of tokens were manifested and promptly shown to you; you must hasten to build a shrine and perform the rites. If you revere me truly, may this place prosper and flourish for all time; I shall also be your guardian deity. Moreover, in Sagami Province there lived a man of the Fujiwara clan bearing the Nishi-Tō name. Invited to serve as head priest, he organized the shrine service. On the twenty-first day of that same month, the sacred rites were performed diligently. The palace, standing facing east before the former horse grounds and extending for several tens of ken, was bordered by rows of trees. In its midst there stood three central torii and two side torii. Notably, one torii was located on the eastern seashore where the tide ebbed; at its base there was a net-like structure. The seashore continued uninterrupted toward the southeast, linking the regions of Anbō and Kazusa. Along the beach, fishermen dwelt and fished. Behind the palace, from the Asabu plateau, a roadway for travelers to the eastern lands was laid out. To the north, in the district of Sakurada, a river flowing there was named Sakuragawa, which eventually merged with a stream that ran by the shrine. Farther northeast, a small stream flowed from behind the palace and ultimately reached the eastern sea. In the vicinity of this river there were abundant rice fields and rustic farmlands, and the lands around the palace were intensively cultivated by many farmers. Some produced confectioneries and were also renowned for growing ginger. Because of the region’s rich harvest of the five grains, the area—since the time the granaries were built—came to be known in local tradition as the “Iikura territory” (and sometimes as Iikura Village). Yet, owing to its humble state, a modest shrine was erected; divine oracles were consulted, and a hereditary priestly family was established to conduct the sacred rites. As years passed, in Jōkyū 4 when General Yoritomo set forth from Nasu-no in Shimotsuke Province, a treasured sword that had been worn became dislodged and sank to the riverbed of the local Utagawa. Despite earnest search and repeated divine consultations, it was never recovered. Meanwhile, near the riverbank, someone proclaimed that a sacred sword—indeed the very one of divine provenance—could be seen gleaming from the turbulent waters. General Yoritomo, upon hearing this, appointed a guide and, accompanied by a retinue, visited the shrine. In due course, he retrieved the sword from the rapids and enshrined it in the treasury of the shrine, so that the divine virtue might be acknowledged. Moreover, a donation of over 1,300 kan of cultivated land was made to the shrine, and in the following year, the roof of the shrine hall was refined and the mansion aligned; henceforth, the local people rejoiced, and the shrine came to be revered as an illustrious emblem of divine favor. |}} }} In the later years of the Edo period, within the urban environs, the shrine—situated on the boundary between the inner city and outlying areas along the {{ill|Tōkaidō|ja|東海道|12=draft}} (with the nearby presence of Kanesugi Bridge) and adjacent to {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|12=draft}}—attracted increasing numbers of worshippers. For travelers leaving Edo, the shrine was a place to pray for a safe journey, while for those entering the city, it offered assurances of safe passage. In addition, although pilgrimage to {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft}} (known as “okage-mairi”) was common in the Edo period, the high cost and long duration of the journey made it difficult for many; as an alternative, many visited this shrine, which enshrines the same deities, right in Edo. As the number of pilgrims grew, a variety of roadside stalls sprang up along the approach – including tea houses, archery stands, blowgun booths, cosmetics stands (known as “hana no tsuyayaya”), sumo rings, conjuring shows, acrobatics, swordsmanship demonstrations, lottery entertainments, and even theaters and other attractions. In particular, the “Taitai Mochi” of Shiba Shinmei became famed as a souvenir. Furthermore, in the Edo period the publisher {{ill|Izumiya Shiheibe|ja|和泉屋市兵衛|12=draft}} – well known as a wholesaler of popular illustrated books – is said to have opened a shop near the shrine during the {{ill|Tenmei|ja|天明|12=draft}} period (1781–89). This area also became a focal point for the mass media. It is also recorded that during the early modern period, beginning with a great fire in the Ōei era (1521–27) originating from a nearby village and several subsequent large fires, the shrine was rebuilt time and again. Among the major reconstructions were: * In Meireki 3 ({{ill|1657|ja|1657|12=draft}}) January, a great fire ({{ill|Meireki Fire|ja|明暦の大火|12=draft}}) razed the buildings; reconstruction began in Kanbun 1 ({{ill|1661|ja|1661|12=draft}}) August. * On {{ill|February 16 (old calendar)|ja|2月16日 (旧暦)|lt=February 16|lt_ja=2月16日|12=draft}} in Hōreki 12 ({{ill|1762|ja|1762|12=draft}}, {{ill|March 11|ja|3月11日|12=draft}}), another great fire occurred; the shrine was rebuilt in Annan 9 ({{ill|1780|ja|1780|12=draft}}) November. * In Bunka 3 on {{ill|March 4 (old calendar)|ja|3月4日 (旧暦)|lt=March 4|lt_ja=3月4日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1806|ja|1806|12=draft}}, {{ill|April 22|ja|4月22日|12=draft}})), a conflagration occurred; again in Bunsei 7 on {{ill|January 5 (old calendar)|ja|1月5日 (旧暦)|lt=January 5|lt_ja=1月5日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1824|ja|1824|12=draft}}, {{ill|February 4|ja|2月4日|12=draft}})); once more in 【Kaei】 3 on {{ill|February 5 (old calendar)|ja|2月5日 (旧暦)|lt=February 5|lt_ja=2月5日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1850|ja|1850|12=draft}}, {{ill|March 18|ja|3月18日|12=draft}})); and finally, in Ansei 2 on {{ill|October 2 (old calendar)|ja|10月2日 (旧暦)|lt=October 2|lt_ja=10月2日|12=draft}} ({{ill|1855|ja|1855|12=draft}}, {{ill|November 11|ja|11月11日|12=draft}})) a major earthquake occurred during reconstruction which led to collapse. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1868|ja|1868|12=draft}}) in October, during the imperial trip of {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|12=draft}}, the main shrine building was temporarily used as the palace for ladies-in-waiting; on {{ill|November 8 (old calendar)|ja|11月8日 (旧暦)|12=draft}}, the shrine was designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft}}, and in the following year ({{ill|1869|ja|1869|12=draft}}) during a long spell of rainy weather, on {{ill|July 3 (old calendar)|ja|7月3日 (旧暦)|lt=July 3|lt_ja=7月3日|12=draft}}, an imperial request was made for prayers to end the rain. However, on {{ill|September 1 (old calendar)|ja|9月1日 (旧暦)|lt=September 1|lt_ja=9月1日|12=draft}} in {{ill|1870|ja|1870|12=draft}} the Associate Imperial Shrine system was abolished, and the shrine became a Prefectural Shrine under Tokyo Prefecture. On January 4, {{ill|1876|ja|1876|12=draft}}, a fire destroyed the building; it was rebuilt in March of the following year ({{ill|1877|ja|1877|12=draft}}). Then in Taishō 12 ({{ill|1923|ja|1923|12=draft}}) on September 1, the Great Kantō Earthquake caused the structure to collapse and burn. In {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和|12=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1927|ja|1927|12=draft}}) in August the main structures were rebuilt, and in Shōwa 13 ({{ill|1938|ja|1938|12=draft}}) in December a complete reconstruction was accomplished. However, on May 26, {{ill|1945|ja|1945|12=draft}}, the building was again destroyed by fire during the Tokyo Air Raid at the end of World War II. In the postwar period the shrine joined the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|12=draft}}, and in Shōwa 22 ({{ill|1947|ja|1947|12=draft}}) on January 13 the main hall was rebuilt; later, in Shōwa 39 ({{ill|1964|ja|1964|12=draft}}) on September 12 the reconstruction was completed, and on September 16, {{ill|Heisei|ja|平成|12=draft}} 17 ({{ill|2005|ja|2005|12=draft}}) during the annual festival a “Shiba Daijingu One-Thousand-Year Festival” was held to celebrate the shrine’s millennium, together with extensive renovations of the administrative office and other structures, forming the present appearance. {{quotation|“'''Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi''' Anko-mochi that has been cherished as a souvenir since the Edo period. It is famously among the offerings of Shiba Shinmei, along with a local folk toy known as the ‘Chikibako’ (a box shaped like a small coin made of wooden planks, arranged in three tiers and bound with straw, on whose surface a wisteria flower is painted in earthen pigment—since the term ‘Chigi’ suggests ‘thousand garments,’ it is said that eating the roasted beans from inside the box will ward off lightning). A paper slip marked “Shiba Miya Taitai Mochi” is also copied.” – Excerpt from Haruharu Shimizu’s _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40), from the section “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library Collection, accessed February 9, 2018.Haruharu Shimizu, _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40): “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library, accessed February 9, 2018}} == Rites == === Priestly Office (Shinto Clergy) === Until the Meiji period, the shrine’s affairs were administered by a threefold system consisting of two families of priests (kamiguji) and a group of temple priests (bettō). The bettō was the chief official. When the shrine was founded, Saiyō Katsutoshi was appointed as the priest; thereafter the Saidō family inherited the priesthood. By the late 11th or early 12th century a separate branch was established, and the priestly office was passed down within the two families – the Saidō and the Koizumi. However, during the Bunsei era (1818–1829) no successor emerged from the separate Saidō branch, so a priest was recruited from the Koizumi family of the Inari shrine at Kitashinagawa (present {{ill|Shinagawa Shrine|ja|品川神社|12=draft}}); the family name remained Koizumi, and from then on the two families, Saidō and Koizumi, shared the priesthood. Under the priests were officials including the Ōnengui (the heads of the Kaburagi family, inherited over generations), the Neigi (a fixed group of seven – from the families of Moriya, Nakahara, Tada, Masuo, Tamekawa, Kōno, and Tanaka, with each head handing down the role), and shrine assistants (from the Kawashima family, inherited over generations). The bettō office, until the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, was located at the temple 【Enryaku-ji】’s branch temple, and later at the branch temple of 【Kannen-ji】 called “Rinkaizan Henjō-ji Kongo-in.” According to temple tradition, this bettō establishment was founded in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|12=draft}} 5 ({{ill|1194|ja|1194|12=draft}}). In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 1 the policy of separating Shinto and Buddhism led to the abolition of the bettō, and the priest became the chief official. In Meiji 5 the title was changed to “Shikikan” (under whom a “Shikashō” was placed), and in Meiji 27 ({{ill|1894|ja|1894|12=draft}}) it was renamed “Shashii” (with a subordinate “Shashō”). In Shōwa 21 (June {{ill|1946|ja|1946|12=draft}}) it was finally reorganized into the present system of the chief priest (宮司) with his assistants. Incidentally, since the Meiji period the priests (or chief priests) have at times been men with experience as senior government officials; for example, {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|ja|稲葉正邦|12=draft}} served from November {{ill|1874|ja|1874|12=draft}} to May {{ill|1878|ja|1878|12=draft}} (as Shikikan), then from July {{ill|1879|ja|1879|12=draft}} to June {{ill|1882|ja|1882|12=draft}}, and again from April {{ill|1882|ja|1882|12=draft}} to November {{ill|1889|ja|1889|12=draft}} (as Shikikan), and from August {{ill|1895|ja|1895|12=draft}} to May {{ill|1897|ja|1897|12=draft}} (as Shashii). In many cases, men of kazoku (nobility) held the office. === Parishioners (Ujiko) === Below is an outline of the various local parish associations and their approximate present-day areas: * Shinbashi Rozuki-chō Neighborhood Association (covering parts of Shinbashi 4‑chome, 5‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 6‑chome Higashi-chō Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome, 6‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 5・6‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome and 6‑chome) * Shinbashi 7‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 6‑chome and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome) * Shibahama Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome and Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome & Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Neighborhood Association * Shibahama 4‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome and Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Kaigan 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (Kaigan 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Kita Shin Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Miyamotochō Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Naka‑ichi Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 1‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Shiba Daimon Naka‑ni Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 2‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Naka‑3 Sanjichi Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 3‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Katamonzen Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome and Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shiba Park 2‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association (formerly known as Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association, Kin San Shinwa Association, Kin Shi Shinsei Jichikai, Kanesugikawaguchi Neighborhood, and Kanehama Shinboku Association; now parts of Shiba 1‑chome and Shiba 2‑chome) * Shiba Niibori Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba 2‑chome and Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba Zaiōji Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 2‑chome) * A portion of Hokushikoku Neighborhood Association (formerly “Sandai Shikoku Higashi-bu”, now part of Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba 3‑chome Matsumoto Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 3‑chome){{Wayback|url=http://www.geocities.jp/mmyosimoto/ |title=芝松本町 |date=20030628112752}} * Shinmonzen Mutsumi Association (formerly “Shiba Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Sanda 1‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 2‑chome Kita Shinmutsumi Association (formerly “Azabu Kita Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Higashi Azabu 2‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 3‑chome Neighborhood Association (formerly “Shinami 1‑chome”, now parts of Higashi Azabu 3‑chome and Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) * A portion of Shin Niikai (formerly “Shinami 2‑chome”, now part of Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) === Annual Events === ; Main Festival (September 16) : Centered on the festival held on September 16, various rituals including mikoshi processions take place from September 11 to 21. Because these events continue “dara dara” (i.e. dragging on) over a long period, the festival has long been known as the “Dara Dara Festival.” In addition, because ginger is distributed during this period, it is also called the “Ginger Festival” (see the section “Offerings” below). ; Savings Festival (October 17) : In commemoration of the achievements of {{ill|Makino Motonanjirō|ja|牧野元次郎|12=draft}} (1874–1942), who established a savings bank (the predecessor of the present {{ill|Resona Bank|ja|りそな銀行|12=draft}}, formerly Asahi Bank and Kyōwa Bank) in the vicinity, a “Savings Mound” (with an inscription by {{ill|Musha Kojii Atsutoku|ja|武者小路実篤|12=draft}}) was erected on the shrine grounds in Shōwa 32 (1957), and ever since, annual prayers for the protection of savings have been conducted. ; Setsubun Festival (February) : On this day the “Hanchō Festival” is held. This ritual is performed by the “Megumi” fire brigade of Edo town—which administers the shrine’s parish area. It is said that during an incident known as the “Megumi Fight” that took place on the shrine grounds in February of Bunka 2 (1805), the ringing of the hanchō (half bell) led to a great commotion. (The hanchō was once exiled but was later returned to the shrine in the Meiji period.) {| border=1 |- | rowspan=2|January || 1 || New Year’s Festival || rowspan=1|June || 30 || Summer Purification Ceremony |- | 2nd Sunday || Coming-of-Age Festival || rowspan=4|September || 3rd Monday || Respect for the Aged Festival |- | rowspan=3|February || 3 || Setsubun Festival || 11–21 || Main Festival |- | 11 || Foundation Festival || 16 || Ritual of the Main Festival |- | 23 || Tenchō Festival (Mid-Rite) || Autumn Equinox || Autumn Equinox Festival |- | rowspan=2|March || 7 || Harvest Prayer Festival (Grand Festival) || rowspan=3|October || 3rd Monday || Sports Festival |- | Vernal Equinox || Vernal Equinox Festival || rowspan=2|17 || Kaminarai Festival |- | rowspan=2|April || 1 || New Enterprise Prayer Festival || Savings Festival |- | 29 || Shōwa Day Festival || rowspan=2|November || 3 || Culture Day Festival |- | rowspan=2|May || 3 || Constitution Memorial Festival || 23 || Niiname Festival (Grand Festival) |- | 5 || Children’s Festival || rowspan=1|December || 31 || New Year Purification Ceremony |} === Kagura (Sacred Dance) === {{Expand section}} == Auxiliary Shrines == In old times many subsidiary (sessha and massha) shrines were located both within and around the grounds, but presently all have been merged into the main shrine. The following describes the situation before the merger. === Within the Shrine Grounds === Until the fire in January {{ill|1876|ja|1876|12=draft}}, the following subsidiary shrines (with their principal deities) were enshrined on the grounds: ; Sessha * {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine|ja|住吉神社|12=draft}} (deities: {{ill|Sumeru no Mikoto|ja|住吉三神|lt=Sumeru deities|lt_ja=表筒男命・中筒男命・底筒男命|12=draft}}) : Formerly known as “Mitarai-sha,” this shrine—located by a pond called Izumigashira—was enshrined as a guardian of the pond. (In the early Meiji period the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Ōwatatsumi no Mikoto|ja|大綿津見命|12=draft}}.) ; Massha * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Kumano Shrine|ja|熊野神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Izanami|ja|伊邪那美命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Suga Shrine|ja|須賀神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|須佐之男命|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt_ja=須佐之男之命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Kotokoronoshi Shrine|ja|事代神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Kensoku Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|健速須佐之男命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Hachiman Shrine|ja|八幡神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Asama Shrine|ja|浅間神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|木花咲耶姫命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Ichikishima Shrine|ja|市杵嶋神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫命|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Suwa Shrine|ja|諏訪神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Tatemikata-no-Kami|ja|建御名方神|lt=Kenmi-no-Kata|lt_ja=健御名方神|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Tenman Shrine|ja|天満神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|Sugawara no Michizane|lt=Sugawara Daijin|lt_ja=菅原大神|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Jitsuro Inari Shrine|ja|実禄稲荷社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Ho-Shokujin|ja|保食神|12=draft}}) * {{ill|Fukushu Inari Shrine|ja|福寿稲荷神社|12=draft}} ({{ill|Wakumusubi|ja|ワクムスヒ|lt=Wakumusubi|lt_ja=和加産毘命|12=draft}}) * Inari Trio – enshrining {{ill|Ukano Mitama|ja|宇賀魂神|12=draft}} After 1876, due to mergers and fires (for example, during the Great Kantō Earthquake), in Shōwa 11 ({{ill|1936|ja|1936|12=draft}}) on September 12 a single subsidiary shrine was rebuilt; with the merger of all the auxiliary shrines, since deities such as {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sukunahikona|ja|少彦名命|1=Sukunabikona|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|12=draft}} were enshrined, the shrine came to be regarded as one that confers protection for milestones (such as 60th, 70th, 77th, or 99th birthdays). Shrine Grounds === * Kaida Inari * U spawn Inari (産千代稲荷) * Shiohiki Inari (潮干稲荷) * Chidō Inari (智童稲荷) == Offerings == * Chigibako (木筥) – The chigibako is said either to have originated from using leftover materials (wooden planks called “chigi” that were used to make a rice container) at the time of the shrine’s construction or from the abbreviation of “mochiki” (a vessel for mounded rice cakes). Today, the chigibako—into which beans are placed—may be hung in a room to ward off lightning. * Shiba Shinmei Ginger – At the time the shrine was founded, the surrounding area was known for its flourishing ginger fields. It is said that ginger was offered before the deity; thereafter, consuming the ginger removed from the altar became reputed to prevent colds, and during the annual festival ginger is again distributed. == Cultural Properties == ; Nagasawa Ashisetsu Painted Portrait (人物図): Tangible Cultural Property (painting) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Colored Paper Mount Hakonoyeizu by Tatebe Suso (建部巣兆筆): Tangible Cultural Property (painting) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kagura Mask with “Kagura Mask Catalogue” attached: Tangible Cultural Property (sculpture) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kagura Mask: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (sculpture) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Ashikaga Naoyoshi’s Teaching Document: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kira Clan Red Seal Document: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Inaha Hanjūrō Chūji Letter: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Sacred Edict: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Document of the Bettō/Priests: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Bronze Lantern: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (historical material) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; The Power Stone of Shiba Daijingu: Tangible Folk Cultural Property designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Hanchō of the Megumi Group: Registered Tangible Folk Cultural Property in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} == Access == * 5‑minute walk from Hamamatsuchō Station on the {{ill|JR Yamanote Line|ja|山手線|12=draft}} and Subway|ja|東京都交通局|12=draft}} – {{ill|Asakusa Line|ja|都営地下鉄浅草線|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oedo Line|ja|都営地下鉄大江戸線|12=draft}}) * 5‑minute walk from Onarimon Station on the Toei Mita Line ({{ill|Toei Subway Mita Line|ja|都営地下鉄三田線|12=draft}}) == References == === Notes === {{notelist}} === Sources === {{reflist|refs= {{Cite web|Writtent {{Shrine |Name = Shiba Daijingu (芝大神宮) |image = [[File:Shiba-daijingu1.jpg|260px|Shiba Daijingu]]
Worship Hall
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=260|coord={{coord|35|39|27.5|N|139|45|11|E}}}} |Location = 1‑12‑7 Shiba Daimon, Minato, Tokyo {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Latitude = 35|Minutes = 39|Seconds = 27.5 |Longitude = 139|Minutes = 45|Seconds = 11 |Enshrined Deities = {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|12=draft|12=draft}}
{{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|12=draft|12=draft}} {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Shrine Rank = Former Prefectural Shrine · {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft|12=draft}} · Tokyo Ten Shrines |Foundation = {{ill|1005|ja|1005|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|12=draft|12=draft}} 2) October 21 |Main Hall = Built in the Shinmei-zukuri style |Alternate Names = Shiba Jinmyōgū · Iikura Jinmyōgū · The Ise of Kanto |Annual Festival = September 16 {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Rituals = Hanchō Festival (February 3)
Dara Dara Festival (September 11–21)
Savings Festival (October 17) }} [[File:Shiba-daijingu 01.jpg|thumb|Worship Hall facing east]] '''Shiba Daijingu''' (芝大神宮) is a {{ill|Shinto Shrine|ja|神社|12=draft|12=draft}} located in 1‑chome of {{ill|Shiba Daimon|ja|芝大門|12=draft|12=draft}}, in {{ill|Minato|ja|港区 (東京都)|lt=Minato|lt_ja=港区|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|12=draft|12=draft}}. At one time it was one of the {{ill|Tokyo Ten Shrines|ja|東京十社|12=draft|12=draft}} designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft|12=draft}}, with its former shrine rank under the modern system being that of a {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|府県社|12=draft|12=draft}}. == 社名 == Originally, the shrine was simply called “Shinmei” or “Shinmeigū.” Because it was once enshrined in Hibiya-gō in {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|12=draft|12=draft}}, it came to be known as “Hibiya Shinmei (Hibiya Shinmeigū)”; and because it was later enshrined at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|12=draft|12=draft}} (later known as Iikura Shō in Musashi Province), it was also called “Iikura Shinmei (Iikura Shinmeigū).” Furthermore, as residents settled in the Shiba area and the town took shape, the name “Shiba Shinmei (Shiba Shinmeigū)” was adopted.{{efn|In Bunsei 10 ({{ill|1827|ja|1827|12=draft|12=draft}}), in the “Temple and Shrine Records” section of the “Document of Geographical Survey of Temples and Shrines” (文政寺社町方書上) compiled for the purpose of the “Gofunai Bikō” ({{ill|Gofunai Bikō|ja|御府内備考|12=draft|12=draft}}) by the Bakufu ({{ill|Bakufu|ja|Tokugawa shogunate|lt=Bakufu|12=draft|12=draft}}), the cover was inscribed “Shiba Shinmeisha,” while the document submitted by the shrine to the Bakufu called it “Iikura Shinmeigū.”}} In addition, because the deities of both the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} are enshrined here, the shrine played a central role in {{ill|Ise Worship|ja|伊勢信仰|12=draft|12=draft}} in the Kantō region and was respectfully called “The Ise of Kanto.” With the advent of the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|12=draft|12=draft}}, and with the approval of the government’s {{ill|Ministry of Religion|ja|教部省|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Daijō-kan Shōin|ja|太政官正院|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Tokyo Prefecture|ja|東京府|12=draft|12=draft}}, from {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 5 ({{ill|August 30 (old calendar)|ja|8月30日 (旧暦)|lt=August 30|lt_ja=8月30日|12=draft|12=draft}}) ({{ill|1872|ja|1872|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 2|ja|10月2日|12=draft|12=draft}}) onward the present name “Shiba Daijingu” was adopted. == {{nihongo|Worshipped deities|祭神|Saijin}} == * {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|12=draft|12=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮内宮|lt=Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=皇大神宮|12=draft|12=draft}}. * {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|12=draft|12=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮外宮|lt=Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=外宮|12=draft|12=draft}}. Unusually for a Tokyo shrine, talismans of Toyouke Ōmikami are also issued. ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|lt_ja=源頼朝公|12=draft|12=draft}} ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|lt_ja=徳川家康公|12=draft|12=draft}} == History == It is said that the shrine traces its origins to a {{ill|Shinmei Shrine|ja|神明社|12=draft|12=draft}} established at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|12=draft|12=draft}} – the kitchen ({{ill|Gochū|ja|御厨|12=draft|12=draft}}) of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} located in Musashi Province – as recorded in the work 『{{ill|Shinpōshō|ja|神鳳鈔|12=draft|12=draft}}』. Initially the shrine was enshrined on Iikura-yama (now, {{ill|Shiba Park|ja|芝公園|12=draft|12=draft}} in Minato). According to the shrine legend, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}, in {{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1005|ja|1005|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 21|ja|10月21日|12=draft|12=draft}}) on {{ill|September 16 (old calendar)|ja|9月16日 (旧暦)|lt=September 16|lt_ja=9月16日|12=draft|12=draft}}, the inner and outer shrines of Ise were enshrined ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}) and a stone known as “Utodoishi” and a sword—both regarded as sacred treasures—were offered. It is said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|12=draft|12=draft}} twice donated shrine domain lands, in {{ill|Genryaku|ja|元暦|12=draft|12=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1185|ja|1185|12=draft|12=draft}}) and in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 ({{ill|1193|ja|1193|12=draft|12=draft}}); in the latter instance, over 1,300 kan of land was donated as a shrine domain ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}). Later in the medieval period the shrine was held in high esteem by the warrior families of eastern Japan. In {{ill|Kenmu|ja|建武|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 on {{ill|January 7 (old calendar)|ja|1月7日 (旧暦)|lt=January 7|lt_ja=1月7日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1337|ja|1337|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|February 8|ja|2月8日|12=draft|12=draft}}), the younger brother of {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|ja|足利尊氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, namely {{ill|Ashikaga Naoyoshi|ja|足利直義|lt=Ashikaga Naoyoshi|lt_ja=直義|12=draft|12=draft}}, offered a letter of reward in recognition of prayers for military success (a document written by Naoyoshi that is preserved at the shrine). During the 【Sengoku period】, the shrine also received veneration from {{ill|Ota Dokan|ja|太田道灌|lt=Ota Dokan|lt_ja=太田資長（道灌）|12=draft|12=draft}}, and in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 16 on {{ill|July 24 (old calendar)|ja|7月24日 (旧暦)|lt=July 24|lt_ja=7月24日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1588|ja|1588|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|September 14|ja|9月14日|12=draft|12=draft}})), an official edict concerning Shibamura was issued by {{ill|Hojo Ujinao|ja|北条氏直|lt=Hojo Ujinao|lt_ja=北条氏直|12=draft|12=draft}} (this edict is also preserved at the shrine). Furthermore, around {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 18 on {{ill|July 19 (old calendar)|ja|7月19日 (旧暦)|lt=July 19|lt_ja=7月19日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1590|ja|1590|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|August 18|ja|8月18日|12=draft|12=draft}})), {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|12=draft|12=draft}} prayed for military victory when dispatching forces from Edo to pacify the Ou region, and in the same year, on {{ill|August 1 (old calendar)|ja|8月1日 (旧暦)|lt=August 1|lt_ja=8月1日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|August 30|ja|8月30日|12=draft|12=draft}}), {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|12=draft|12=draft}} visited the shrine upon his entry into Edo; then, in the following year on {{ill|November 28 (old calendar)|ja|11月28日 (旧暦)|lt=November 28|lt_ja=11月28日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1592|ja|1592|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|January 12|ja|1月12日|12=draft|12=draft}})), he donated 15 koku of land in Hibiya of Musashi Province as shrine domain. In {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長|12=draft|12=draft}} 3 (1598) in August, when {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|12=draft|12=draft}} was relocated from the shrine’s former site (Shiba Park), the shrine was moved to its present location (Shiba Daimon, Minato). In the 5th year ({{ill|1600|ja|1600|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|October 7|ja|10月7日|12=draft|12=draft}}) following the move, Ieyasu himself visited the shrine on his way to the {{ill|Battle of Sekigahara|ja|関ヶ原の戦い|lt=Sekigahara|lt_ja=関ヶ原|12=draft|12=draft}} to pray for victory; and during the Siege of Osaka in the 19th to 20th years, as a proxy for the shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|ja|徳川秀忠|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|lt_ja=秀忠|12=draft|12=draft}}’s principal wife Oeyo ({{ill|Sūgen-in|ja|崇源院|12=draft|12=draft}}), the nurse of {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|ja|徳川家光|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|lt_ja=家光|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Kasuga no Tsubone|ja|春日局|12=draft|12=draft}} made a shrine visit. Thereafter, under the patronage of successive shōguns and the Bakufu, the construction and repair of the shrine buildings were executed by imperial orders, and various prayer requests were received from the Bakufu (for example, a prayer for safe delivery on the occasion of the birth of the 4th shōgun, {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|12=draft|12=draft}}) – and the shrine was also revered by feudal lords and other regional authorities (for instance, repairs to the shrine buildings were undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Fukui Domain, and the lord of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|lt=Satsuma Domain Lord|lt_ja=薩摩藩主|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|12=draft|12=draft}}, enshrined the deity in Kagoshima (presently at {{ill|Taga Shrine|ja|多賀神社 (鹿児島市)|lt=Taga Shrine|lt_ja=多賀神社|12=draft|12=draft}} in Shimizu-cho, Kagoshima City)).{{efn|Examples include the safe-delivery prayer for the birth of the 4th shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|12=draft|12=draft}}, and the shrine repairs undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|12=draft|12=draft}} of the Echizen Fukui Domain, as well as the enshrinement by the lord of the Satsuma Domain, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|12=draft|12=draft}}, in Kagoshima.}} {{efn|Regarding the above, the following is an excerpt from the “Bunsei Jūnen Shojō” (文政十年書上) that records the shrine’s founding legend for reference: {{Quotation| The origin of enshrining the twin deities at the Great Shrine in Hibiya-gō of Toyoshima District in Musashi Province is said to date from the sixteenth day of September in the second year of Kankō during the reign of Emperor Ichijō. On that day, a sacred token together with a large fang descended upon this place. All the village’s elders, youths, and children gathered, and though they were at first suspicious of the seemingly miraculous descent of this divine token of Shinmei, a little girl inexplicably approached. Her face changed as she hurriedly proclaimed, “I am the divine wind—the deity of both the inner and outer shrines of Ise—and because there is military strife in these eastern lands, I have come down to subdue the armies and mark this place as my dwelling.” Thus, two types of tokens were manifested and promptly shown to you; you must hasten to build a shrine and perform the rites. If you revere me truly, may this place prosper and flourish for all time; I shall also be your guardian deity. Moreover, in Sagami Province there lived a man of the Fujiwara clan bearing the Nishi-Tō name. Invited to serve as head priest, he organized the shrine service. On the twenty-first day of that same month, the sacred rites were performed diligently. The palace, standing facing east before the former horse grounds and extending for several tens of ken, was bordered by rows of trees. In its midst there stood three central torii and two side torii. Notably, one torii was located on the eastern seashore where the tide ebbed; at its base there was a net-like structure. The seashore continued uninterrupted toward the southeast, linking the regions of Anbō and Kazusa. Along the beach, fishermen dwelt and fished. Behind the palace, from the Asabu plateau, a roadway for travelers to the eastern lands was laid out. To the north, in the district of Sakurada, a river flowing there was named Sakuragawa, which eventually merged with a stream that ran by the shrine. Farther northeast, a small stream flowed from behind the palace and ultimately reached the eastern sea. In the vicinity of this river there were abundant rice fields and rustic farmlands, and the lands around the palace were intensively cultivated by many farmers. Some produced confectioneries and were also renowned for growing ginger. Because of the region’s rich harvest of the five grains, the area—since the time the granaries were built—came to be known in local tradition as the “Iikura territory” (and sometimes as Iikura Village). Yet, owing to its humble state, a modest shrine was erected; divine oracles were consulted, and a hereditary priestly family was established to conduct the sacred rites. As years passed, in Jōkyū 4 when General Yoritomo set forth from Nasu-no in Shimotsuke Province, a treasured sword that had been worn became dislodged and sank to the riverbed of the local Utagawa. Despite earnest search and repeated divine consultations, it was never recovered. Meanwhile, near the riverbank, someone proclaimed that a sacred sword—indeed the very one of divine provenance—could be seen gleaming from the turbulent waters. General Yoritomo, upon hearing this, appointed a guide and, accompanied by a retinue, visited the shrine. In due course, he retrieved the sword from the rapids and enshrined it in the treasury of the shrine, so that the divine virtue might be acknowledged. Moreover, a donation of over 1,300 kan of cultivated land was made to the shrine, and in the following year, the roof of the shrine hall was refined and the mansion aligned; henceforth, the local people rejoiced, and the shrine came to be revered as an illustrious emblem of divine favor. |}} }} In the later years of the Edo period, within the urban environs, the shrine—situated on the boundary between the inner city and outlying areas along the {{ill|Tōkaidō|ja|東海道|12=draft|12=draft}} (with the nearby presence of Kanesugi Bridge) and adjacent to {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|12=draft|12=draft}}—attracted increasing numbers of worshippers. For travelers leaving Edo, the shrine was a place to pray for a safe journey, while for those entering the city, it offered assurances of safe passage. In addition, although pilgrimage to {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|12=draft|12=draft}} (known as “okage-mairi”) was common in the Edo period, the high cost and long duration of the journey made it difficult for many; as an alternative, many visited this shrine, which enshrines the same deities, right in Edo. As the number of pilgrims grew, a variety of roadside stalls sprang up along the approach – including tea houses, archery stands, blowgun booths, cosmetics stands (known as “hana no tsuyayaya”), sumo rings, conjuring shows, acrobatics, swordsmanship demonstrations, lottery entertainments, and even theaters and other attractions. In particular, the “Taitai Mochi” of Shiba Shinmei became famed as a souvenir. Furthermore, in the Edo period the publisher {{ill|Izumiya Shiheibe|ja|和泉屋市兵衛|12=draft|12=draft}} – well known as a wholesaler of popular illustrated books – is said to have opened a shop near the shrine during the {{ill|Tenmei|ja|天明|12=draft|12=draft}} period (1781–89). This area also became a focal point for the mass media. It is also recorded that during the early modern period, beginning with a great fire in the Ōei era (1521–27) originating from a nearby village and several subsequent large fires, the shrine was rebuilt time and again. Among the major reconstructions were: * In Meireki 3 ({{ill|1657|ja|1657|12=draft|12=draft}}) January, a great fire ({{ill|Meireki Fire|ja|明暦の大火|12=draft|12=draft}}) razed the buildings; reconstruction began in Kanbun 1 ({{ill|1661|ja|1661|12=draft|12=draft}}) August. * On {{ill|February 16 (old calendar)|ja|2月16日 (旧暦)|lt=February 16|lt_ja=2月16日|12=draft|12=draft}} in Hōreki 12 ({{ill|1762|ja|1762|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|March 11|ja|3月11日|12=draft|12=draft}}), another great fire occurred; the shrine was rebuilt in Annan 9 ({{ill|1780|ja|1780|12=draft|12=draft}}) November. * In Bunka 3 on {{ill|March 4 (old calendar)|ja|3月4日 (旧暦)|lt=March 4|lt_ja=3月4日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1806|ja|1806|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|April 22|ja|4月22日|12=draft|12=draft}})), a conflagration occurred; again in Bunsei 7 on {{ill|January 5 (old calendar)|ja|1月5日 (旧暦)|lt=January 5|lt_ja=1月5日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1824|ja|1824|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|February 4|ja|2月4日|12=draft|12=draft}})); once more in 【Kaei】 3 on {{ill|February 5 (old calendar)|ja|2月5日 (旧暦)|lt=February 5|lt_ja=2月5日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1850|ja|1850|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|March 18|ja|3月18日|12=draft|12=draft}})); and finally, in Ansei 2 on {{ill|October 2 (old calendar)|ja|10月2日 (旧暦)|lt=October 2|lt_ja=10月2日|12=draft|12=draft}} ({{ill|1855|ja|1855|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|November 11|ja|11月11日|12=draft|12=draft}})) a major earthquake occurred during reconstruction which led to collapse. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1868|ja|1868|12=draft|12=draft}}) in October, during the imperial trip of {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|12=draft|12=draft}}, the main shrine building was temporarily used as the palace for ladies-in-waiting; on {{ill|November 8 (old calendar)|ja|11月8日 (旧暦)|12=draft|12=draft}}, the shrine was designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|12=draft|12=draft}}, and in the following year ({{ill|1869|ja|1869|12=draft|12=draft}}) during a long spell of rainy weather, on {{ill|July 3 (old calendar)|ja|7月3日 (旧暦)|lt=July 3|lt_ja=7月3日|12=draft|12=draft}}, an imperial request was made for prayers to end the rain. However, on {{ill|September 1 (old calendar)|ja|9月1日 (旧暦)|lt=September 1|lt_ja=9月1日|12=draft|12=draft}} in {{ill|1870|ja|1870|12=draft|12=draft}} the Associate Imperial Shrine system was abolished, and the shrine became a Prefectural Shrine under Tokyo Prefecture. On January 4, {{ill|1876|ja|1876|12=draft|12=draft}}, a fire destroyed the building; it was rebuilt in March of the following year ({{ill|1877|ja|1877|12=draft|12=draft}}). Then in Taishō 12 ({{ill|1923|ja|1923|12=draft|12=draft}}) on September 1, the Great Kantō Earthquake caused the structure to collapse and burn. In {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1927|ja|1927|12=draft|12=draft}}) in August the main structures were rebuilt, and in Shōwa 13 ({{ill|1938|ja|1938|12=draft|12=draft}}) in December a complete reconstruction was accomplished. However, on May 26, {{ill|1945|ja|1945|12=draft|12=draft}}, the building was again destroyed by fire during the Tokyo Air Raid at the end of World War II. In the postwar period the shrine joined the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|12=draft|12=draft}}, and in Shōwa 22 ({{ill|1947|ja|1947|12=draft|12=draft}}) on January 13 the main hall was rebuilt; later, in Shōwa 39 ({{ill|1964|ja|1964|12=draft|12=draft}}) on September 12 the reconstruction was completed, and on September 16, {{ill|Heisei|ja|平成|12=draft|12=draft}} 17 ({{ill|2005|ja|2005|12=draft|12=draft}}) during the annual festival a “Shiba Daijingu One-Thousand-Year Festival” was held to celebrate the shrine’s millennium, together with extensive renovations of the administrative office and other structures, forming the present appearance. {{quotation|“'''Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi''' Anko-mochi that has been cherished as a souvenir since the Edo period. It is famously among the offerings of Shiba Shinmei, along with a local folk toy known as the ‘Chikibako’ (a box shaped like a small coin made of wooden planks, arranged in three tiers and bound with straw, on whose surface a wisteria flower is painted in earthen pigment—since the term ‘Chigi’ suggests ‘thousand garments,’ it is said that eating the roasted beans from inside the box will ward off lightning). A paper slip marked “Shiba Miya Taitai Mochi” is also copied.” – Excerpt from Haruharu Shimizu’s _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40), from the section “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library Collection, accessed February 9, 2018.Haruharu Shimizu, _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40): “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library, accessed February 9, 2018}} == Rites == === Priestly Office (Shinto Clergy) === Until the Meiji period, the shrine’s affairs were administered by a threefold system consisting of two families of priests (kamiguji) and a group of temple priests (bettō). The bettō was the chief official. When the shrine was founded, Saiyō Katsutoshi was appointed as the priest; thereafter the Saidō family inherited the priesthood. By the late 11th or early 12th century a separate branch was established, and the priestly office was passed down within the two families – the Saidō and the Koizumi. However, during the Bunsei era (1818–1829) no successor emerged from the separate Saidō branch, so a priest was recruited from the Koizumi family of the Inari shrine at Kitashinagawa (present {{ill|Shinagawa Shrine|ja|品川神社|12=draft|12=draft}}); the family name remained Koizumi, and from then on the two families, Saidō and Koizumi, shared the priesthood. Under the priests were officials including the Ōnengui (the heads of the Kaburagi family, inherited over generations), the Neigi (a fixed group of seven – from the families of Moriya, Nakahara, Tada, Masuo, Tamekawa, Kōno, and Tanaka, with each head handing down the role), and shrine assistants (from the Kawashima family, inherited over generations). The bettō office, until the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, was located at the temple 【Enryaku-ji】’s branch temple, and later at the branch temple of 【Kannen-ji】 called “Rinkaizan Henjō-ji Kongo-in.” According to temple tradition, this bettō establishment was founded in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|12=draft|12=draft}} 5 ({{ill|1194|ja|1194|12=draft|12=draft}}). In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 1 the policy of separating Shinto and Buddhism led to the abolition of the bettō, and the priest became the chief official. In Meiji 5 the title was changed to “Shikikan” (under whom a “Shikashō” was placed), and in Meiji 27 ({{ill|1894|ja|1894|12=draft|12=draft}}) it was renamed “Shashii” (with a subordinate “Shashō”). In Shōwa 21 (June {{ill|1946|ja|1946|12=draft|12=draft}}) it was finally reorganized into the present system of the chief priest (宮司) with his assistants. Incidentally, since the Meiji period the priests (or chief priests) have at times been men with experience as senior government officials; for example, {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|ja|稲葉正邦|12=draft|12=draft}} served from November {{ill|1874|ja|1874|12=draft|12=draft}} to May {{ill|1878|ja|1878|12=draft|12=draft}} (as Shikikan), then from July {{ill|1879|ja|1879|12=draft|12=draft}} to June {{ill|1882|ja|1882|12=draft|12=draft}}, and again from April {{ill|1882|ja|1882|12=draft|12=draft}} to November {{ill|1889|ja|1889|12=draft|12=draft}} (as Shikikan), and from August {{ill|1895|ja|1895|12=draft|12=draft}} to May {{ill|1897|ja|1897|12=draft|12=draft}} (as Shashii). In many cases, men of kazoku (nobility) held the office. === Parishioners (Ujiko) === Below is an outline of the various local parish associations and their approximate present-day areas: * Shinbashi Rozuki-chō Neighborhood Association (covering parts of Shinbashi 4‑chome, 5‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 6‑chome Higashi-chō Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome, 6‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 5・6‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome and 6‑chome) * Shinbashi 7‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 6‑chome and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome) * Shibahama Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome and Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome & Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Neighborhood Association * Shibahama 4‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome and Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Kaigan 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (Kaigan 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Kita Shin Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Miyamotochō Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Naka‑ichi Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 1‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Shiba Daimon Naka‑ni Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 2‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Naka‑3 Sanjichi Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 3‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Katamonzen Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome and Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shiba Park 2‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association (formerly known as Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association, Kin San Shinwa Association, Kin Shi Shinsei Jichikai, Kanesugikawaguchi Neighborhood, and Kanehama Shinboku Association; Main Festival (September 16) : Centered on the festival held on September 16, various rituals including mikoshi processions take place from September 11 to 21. Because these events continue “dara dara” (i.e. dragging on) over a long period, the festival has long been known as the “Dara Dara Festival.” In addition, because ginger is distributed during this period, it is also called the “Ginger Festival” (see the section “Offerings” below). ; Savings Festival (October 17) : In commemoration of the achievements of {{ill|Makino Motonanjirō|ja|牧野元次郎|12=draft|12=draft}} (1874–1942), who established a savings bank (the predecessor of the present {{ill|Resona Bank|ja|りそな銀行|12=draft|12=draft}}, formerly Asahi Bank and Kyōwa Bank) in the vicinity, a “Savings Mound” (with an inscription by {{ill|Musha Kojii Atsutoku|ja|武者小路実篤|12=draft|12=draft}}) was erected on the shrine grounds in Shōwa 32 (1957), and ever since, annual prayers for the protection of savings have been conducted. ; Setsubun Festival (February) : On this day the “Hanchō Festival” is held. This ritual is performed by the “Megumi” fire brigade of Edo town—which administers the shrine’s parish area. It is said that during an incident known as the “Megumi Fight” that took place on the shrine grounds in February of Bunka 2 (1805), the ringing of the hanchō (half bell) led to a great commotion. (智童稲荷) == Offerings == * Chigibako (木筥) – The chigibako is said either to have originated from using leftover materials (wooden planks called “chigi” that were used to make a rice container) at the time of the shrine’s construction or from the abbreviation of “mochiki” (a vessel for mounded rice cakes). Today, the chigibako—into which beans are placed—may be hung in a room to ward off lightning. * Shiba Shinmei Ginger – At the time the shrine was founded, the surrounding area was known for its flourishing ginger fields. It is said that ginger was offered before the deity; thereafter, consuming the ginger removed from the altar became reputed to prevent colds, and during the annual festival ginger is again
