{{Shrine |Name = Shiba Daijingu (芝大神宮) |image = [[File:Shiba-daijingu1.jpg|260px|Shiba Daijingu]]
Worship Hall
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=260|coord={{coord|35|39|27.5|N|139|45|11|E}}}} |Location = 1‑12‑7 Shiba Daimon, Minato, Tokyo {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Latitude = 35|Minutes = 39|Seconds = 27.5 |Longitude = 139|Minutes = 45|Seconds = 11 |Enshrined Deities = {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
{{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Shrine Rank = Former Prefectural Shrine · {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} · Tokyo Ten Shrines |Foundation = {{ill|1005|ja|1005|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2) October 21 |Main Hall = Built in the Shinmei-zukuri style |Alternate Names = Shiba Jinmyōgū · Iikura Jinmyōgū · The Ise of Kanto |Annual Festival = September 16 {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Rituals = Hanchō Festival (February 3)
Dara Dara Festival (September 11–21)
Savings Festival (October 17) }} [[File:Shiba-daijingu 01.jpg|thumb|Worship Hall facing east]] '''Shiba Daijingu''' (芝大神宮) is a {{ill|Shinto Shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in 1‑chome of {{ill|Shiba Daimon|ja|芝大門|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in {{ill|Minato|ja|港区 (東京都)|lt=Minato|lt_ja=港区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. At one time it was one of the {{ill|Tokyo Ten Shrines|ja|東京十社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with its former shrine Rank under the modern system being that of a {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|府県社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. == 社名 == Originally, the shrine was simply called “Shinmei” or “Shinmeigū.” Because it was once enshrined in Hibiya-gō in {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it came to be known as “Hibiya Shinmei (Hibiya Shinmeigū)”; and because it was later enshrined at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (later known as Iikura Shō in Musashi Province), it was also called “Iikura Shinmei (Iikura Shinmeigū).” Furthermore, as residents settled in the Shiba area and the town took shape, the name “Shiba Shinmei (Shiba Shinmeigū)” was adopted.{{efn|In Bunsei 10 ({{ill|1827|ja|1827|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), in the “Temple and Shrine Records” section of the “Document of Geographical Survey of Temples and Shrines” (文政寺社町方書上) compiled for the purpose of the “Gofunai Bikō” ({{ill|Gofunai Bikō|ja|御府内備考|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by the Bakufu ({{ill|Bakufu|ja|Tokugawa shogunate|lt=Bakufu|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the cover was inscribed “Shiba Shinmeisha,” while the document submitted by the shrine to the Bakufu called it “Iikura Shinmeigū.”}} In addition, because the deities of both the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are enshrined here, the shrine played a central role in {{ill|Ise Worship|ja|伊勢信仰|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Kantō region and was respectfully called “The Ise of Kanto.” With the advent of the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and with the approval of the government’s {{ill|Ministry of Religion|ja|教部省|1=Ministry of Religion (Japan)|lt=Ministry of Religion|qq= (Japan)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Daijō-kan Shōin|ja|太政官正院|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tokyo Prefecture|ja|東京府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, from {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 5 ({{ill|August 30 (old calendar)|ja|8月30日 (旧暦)|lt=August 30|lt_ja=8月30日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) ({{ill|1872|ja|1872|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 2|ja|10月2日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) onward the present name “Shiba Daijingu” was adopted. == {{nihongo|Worshipped deities|祭神|Saijin}} == * {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮内宮|lt=Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮外宮|lt=Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=外宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Unusually for a Tokyo shrine, talismans of Toyouke Ōmikami are also issued. ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|lt_ja=源頼朝公|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|lt_ja=徳川家康公|qq=draft|qq=draft}} == History == It is said that the shrine traces its origins to a {{ill|Shinmei Shrine|ja|神明社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the kitchen ({{ill|Gochū|ja|御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in Musashi Province – as recorded in the work 『{{ill|Shinpōshō|ja|神鳳鈔|qq=draft|qq=draft}}』. Initially the shrine was enshrined on Iikura-yama (now, {{ill|Shiba Park|ja|芝公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Minato). According to the shrine legend, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in {{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1005|ja|1005|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 21|ja|10月21日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on {{ill|September 16 (old calendar)|ja|9月16日 (旧暦)|lt=September 16|lt_ja=9月16日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the inner and outer shrines of Ise were enshrined ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}) and a stone known as “Utodoishi” and a sword—both regarded as sacred treasures—were offered. It is said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} twice donated shrine domain lands, in {{ill|Genryaku|ja|元暦|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1185|ja|1185|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 4 ({{ill|1193|ja|1193|qq=draft|qq=draft}}); in the latter instance, over 1,300 kan of land was donated as a shrine domain ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}). Later in the medieval period the shrine was held in high esteem by the warrior families of eastern Japan. In {{ill|Kenmu|ja|建武|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 4 on {{ill|January 7 (old calendar)|ja|1月7日 (旧暦)|lt=January 7|lt_ja=1月7日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1337|ja|1337|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|February 8|ja|2月8日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the younger brother of {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|ja|足利尊氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, namely {{ill|Ashikaga Naoyoshi|ja|足利直義|lt=Ashikaga Naoyoshi|lt_ja=直義|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, offered a letter of reward in recognition of prayers for military success (a document written by Naoyoshi that is preserved at the shrine). During the 【Sengoku period】, the shrine also received veneration from {{ill|Ota Dokan|ja|太田道灌|lt=Ota Dokan|lt_ja=太田資長（道灌）|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 16 on {{ill|July 24 (old calendar)|ja|7月24日 (旧暦)|lt=July 24|lt_ja=7月24日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1588|ja|1588|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|September 14|ja|9月14日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), an official edict concerning Shibamura was issued by {{ill|Hojo Ujinao|ja|北条氏直|lt=Hojo Ujinao|lt_ja=北条氏直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (this edict is also preserved at the shrine). Furthermore, around {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 18 on {{ill|July 19 (old calendar)|ja|7月19日 (旧暦)|lt=July 19|lt_ja=7月19日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1590|ja|1590|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|August 18|ja|8月18日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for military victory when dispatching forces from Edo to pacify the Ou region, and in the same year, on {{ill|August 1 (old calendar)|ja|8月1日 (旧暦)|lt=August 1|lt_ja=8月1日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|August 30|ja|8月30日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|qq=draft|qq=draft}} visited the shrine upon his entry into Edo; then, in the following year on {{ill|November 28 (old calendar)|ja|11月28日 (旧暦)|lt=November 28|lt_ja=11月28日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1592|ja|1592|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|January 12|ja|1月12日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), he donated 15 koku of land in Hibiya of Musashi Province as shrine domain. In {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 3 (1598) in August, when {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was relocated from the shrine’s former site (Shiba Park), the shrine was moved to its present location (Shiba Daimon, Minato). In the 5th year ({{ill|1600|ja|1600|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 7|ja|10月7日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) following the move, Ieyasu himself visited the shrine on his way to the {{ill|Battle of Sekigahara|ja|関ヶ原の戦い|lt=Sekigahara|lt_ja=関ヶ原|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to pray for victory; and during the Siege of Osaka in the 19th to 20th years, as a proxy for the shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|ja|徳川秀忠|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|lt_ja=秀忠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s principal wife Oeyo ({{ill|Sūgen-in|ja|崇源院|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the nurse of {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|ja|徳川家光|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|lt_ja=家光|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kasuga no Tsubone|ja|春日局|qq=draft|qq=draft}} made a shrine visit. Thereafter, under the patronage of successive shōguns and the Bakufu, the construction and repair of the shrine buildings were executed by imperial orders, and various prayer requests were received from the Bakufu (for example, a prayer for safe delivery on the occasion of the birth of the 4th shōgun, {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) – and the shrine was also revered by feudal lords and other regional authorities (for instance, repairs to the shrine buildings were undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the Fukui Domain, and the lord of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|lt=Satsuma Domain Lord|lt_ja=薩摩藩主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, enshrined the deity in Kagoshima (presently at {{ill|Taga Shrine|ja|多賀神社 (鹿児島市)|lt=Taga Shrine|lt_ja=多賀神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Shimizu-cho, Kagoshima City)).{{efn|Examples include the safe-delivery prayer for the birth of the 4th shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and the shrine repairs undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the Echizen Fukui Domain, as well as the enshrinement by the lord of the Satsuma Domain, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in Kagoshima.}} {{efn|Regarding the above, the following is an excerpt from the “Bunsei Jūnen Shojō” (文政十年書上) that records the shrine’s founding legend for reference: {{Quotation| The origin of enshrining the twin deities at the Great Shrine in Hibiya-gō of Toyoshima District in Musashi Province is said to date from the sixteenth day of September in the second year of Kankō during the reign of Emperor Ichijō. On that day, a sacred token together with a large fang descended upon this place. All the village’s elders, youths, and children gathered, and though they were at first suspicious of the seemingly miraculous descent of this divine token of Shinmei, a little girl inexplicably approached. Her face changed as she hurriedly proclaimed, “I am the divine wind—the deity of both the inner and outer shrines of Ise—and because there is military strife in these eastern lands, I have come down to subdue the armies and mark this place as my dwelling.” Thus, two types of tokens were manifested and promptly shown to you; you must hasten to build a shrine and perform the rites. If you revere me truly, may this place prosper and flourish for all time; I shall also be your guardian deity. Moreover, in Sagami Province there lived a man of the Fujiwara clan bearing the Nishi-Tō name. Invited to serve as head priest, he organized the shrine service. On the twenty-first day of that same month, the sacred rites were performed diligently. The palace, standing facing east before the former horse grounds and extending for several tens of ken, was bordered by rows of trees. In its midst there stood three central torii and two side torii. Notably, one torii was located on the eastern seashore where the tide ebbed; at its base there was a net-like structure. The seashore continued uninterrupted toward the southeast, linking the regions of Anbō and Kazusa. Along the beach, fishermen dwelt and fished. Behind the palace, from the Asabu plateau, a roadway for travelers to the eastern lands was laid out. To the north, in the district of Sakurada, a river flowing there was named Sakuragawa, which eventually merged with a stream that ran by the shrine. Farther northeast, a small stream flowed from behind the palace and ultimately reached the eastern sea. In the vicinity of this river there were abundant rice fields and rustic farmlands, and the lands around the palace were intensively cultivated by many farmers. Some produced confectioneries and were also renowned for growing ginger. Because of the region’s rich harvest of the five grains, the area—since the time the granaries were built—came to be known in local tradition as the “Iikura territory” (and sometimes as Iikura Village). Yet, owing to its humble state, a modest shrine was erected; divine oracles were consulted, and a hereditary priestly family was established to conduct the sacred rites. As years passed, in Jōkyū 4 when General Yoritomo set forth from Nasu-no in Shimotsuke Province, a treasured sword that had been worn became dislodged and sank to the riverbed of the local Utagawa. Despite earnest search and repeated divine consultations, it was never recovered. Meanwhile, near the riverbank, someone proclaimed that a sacred sword—indeed the very one of divine provenance—could be seen gleaming from the turbulent waters. General Yoritomo, upon hearing this, appointed a guide and, accompanied by a retinue, visited the shrine. In due course, he retrieved the sword from the rapids and enshrined it in the treasury of the shrine, so that the divine virtue might be acknowledged. Moreover, a donation of over 1,300 kan of cultivated land was made to the shrine, and in the following year, the roof of the shrine hall was refined and the mansion aligned; henceforth, the local people rejoiced, and the shrine came to be revered as an illustrious emblem of divine favor. |}} }} In the later years of the Edo period, within the urban environs, the shrine—situated on the boundary between the inner city and outlying areas along the {{ill|Tōkaidō|ja|東海道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (with the nearby presence of Kanesugi Bridge) and adjacent to {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—attracted increasing numbers of worshippers. For travelers leaving Edo, the shrine was a place to pray for a safe journey, while for those entering the city, it offered assurances of safe passage. In addition, although pilgrimage to {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (known as “okage-mairi”) was common in the Edo period, the high cost and long duration of the journey made it difficult for many; as an alternative, many visited this shrine, which enshrines the same deities, right in Edo. As the number of pilgrims grew, a variety of roadside stalls sprang up along the approach – including tea houses, archery stands, blowgun booths, cosmetics stands (known as “hana no tsuyayaya”), sumo rings, conjuring shows, acrobatics, swordsmanship demonstrations, lottery entertainments, and even theaters and other attractions. In particular, the “Taitai Mochi” of Shiba Shinmei became famed as a souvenir. Furthermore, in the Edo period the publisher {{ill|Izumiya Shiheibe|ja|和泉屋市兵衛|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – well known as a wholesaler of popular illustrated books – is said to have opened a shop near the shrine during the {{ill|Tenmei|ja|天明|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period (1781–89). This area also became a focal point for the mass media. It is also recorded that during the early modern period, beginning with a great fire in the Ōei era (1521–27) originating from a nearby village and several subsequent large fires, the shrine was rebuilt time and again. Among the major reconstructions were: * In Meireki 3 ({{ill|1657|ja|1657|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) January, a great fire ({{ill|Meireki Fire|ja|明暦の大火|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) razed the buildings; reconstruction began in Kanbun 1 ({{ill|1661|ja|1661|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) August. * On {{ill|February 16 (old calendar)|ja|2月16日 (旧暦)|lt=February 16|lt_ja=2月16日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hōreki 12 ({{ill|1762|ja|1762|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|March 11|ja|3月11日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), another great fire occurred; the shrine was rebuilt in Annan 9 ({{ill|1780|ja|1780|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) November. * In Bunka 3 on {{ill|March 4 (old calendar)|ja|3月4日 (旧暦)|lt=March 4|lt_ja=3月4日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1806|ja|1806|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|April 22|ja|4月22日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), a conflagration occurred; again in Bunsei 7 on {{ill|January 5 (old calendar)|ja|1月5日 (旧暦)|lt=January 5|lt_ja=1月5日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1824|ja|1824|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|February 4|ja|2月4日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})); once more in 【Kaei】 3 on {{ill|February 5 (old calendar)|ja|2月5日 (旧暦)|lt=February 5|lt_ja=2月5日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1850|ja|1850|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|March 18|ja|3月18日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})); and finally, in Ansei 2 on {{ill|October 2 (old calendar)|ja|10月2日 (旧暦)|lt=October 2|lt_ja=10月2日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1855|ja|1855|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|November 11|ja|11月11日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})) a major earthquake occurred during reconstruction which led to collapse. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1868|ja|1868|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in October, during the imperial trip of {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the main shrine building was temporarily used as the palace for ladies-in-waiting; on {{ill|November 8 (old calendar)|ja|11月8日 (旧暦)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the shrine was designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the following year ({{ill|1869|ja|1869|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) during a long spell of rainy weather, on {{ill|July 3 (old calendar)|ja|7月3日 (旧暦)|lt=July 3|lt_ja=7月3日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, an imperial request was made for prayers to end the rain. However, on {{ill|September 1 (old calendar)|ja|9月1日 (旧暦)|lt=September 1|lt_ja=9月1日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|1870|ja|1870|qq=draft|qq=draft}} the Associate Imperial Shrine system was abolished, and the shrine became a Prefectural Shrine under Tokyo Prefecture. On January 4, {{ill|1876|ja|1876|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a fire destroyed the building; it was rebuilt in March of the following year ({{ill|1877|ja|1877|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Then in Taishō 12 ({{ill|1923|ja|1923|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 1, the Great Kantō Earthquake caused the structure to collapse and burn. In {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1927|ja|1927|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in August the main structures were rebuilt, and in Shōwa 13 ({{ill|1938|ja|1938|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in December a complete reconstruction was accomplished. However, on May 26, {{ill|1945|ja|1945|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the building was again destroyed by fire during the Tokyo Air Raid at the end of World War II. In the postwar period the shrine joined the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in Shōwa 22 ({{ill|1947|ja|1947|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on January 13 the main hall was rebuilt; later, in Shōwa 39 ({{ill|1964|ja|1964|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 12 the reconstruction was completed, and on September 16, {{ill|Heisei|ja|平成|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 17 ({{ill|2005|ja|2005|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) during the annual festival a “Shiba Daijingu One-Thousand-Year Festival” was held to celebrate the shrine’s millennium, together with extensive renovations of the administrative office and other structures, forming the present appearance. {{quotation|“'''Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi''' Anko-mochi that has been cherished as a souvenir since the Edo period. It is famously among the offerings of Shiba Shinmei, along with a local folk toy known as the ‘Chikibako’ (a box shaped like a small coin made of wooden planks, arranged in three tiers and bound with straw, on whose surface a wisteria flower is painted in earthen pigment—since the term ‘Chigi’ suggests ‘thousand garments,’ it is said that eating the roasted beans from inside the box will ward off lightning). A paper slip marked “Shiba Miya Taitai Mochi” is also copied.” – Excerpt from Haruharu Shimizu’s _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40), from the section “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library Collection, accessed February 9, 2018.Haruharu Shimizu, _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40): “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library, accessed February 9, 2018}} == Rites == === Priestly Office (Shinto Clergy) === Until the Meiji period, the shrine’s affairs were administered by a threefold system consisting of two families of priests (kamiguji) and a group of temple priests (bettō). The bettō was the chief official. When the shrine was founded, Saiyō Katsutoshi was appointed as the priest; thereafter the Saidō family inherited the priesthood. By the late 11th or early 12th century a separate branch was established, and the priestly office was passed down within the two families – the Saidō and the Koizumi. However, during the Bunsei era (1818–1829) no successor emerged from the separate Saidō branch, so a priest was recruited from the Koizumi family of the Inari shrine at Kitashinagawa (present {{ill|Shinagawa Shrine|ja|品川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}); the family name remained Koizumi, and from then on the two families, Saidō and Koizumi, shared the priesthood. Under the priests were officials including the Ōnengui (the heads of the Kaburagi family, inherited over generations), the Neigi (a fixed group of seven – from the families of Moriya, Nakahara, Tada, Masuo, Tamekawa, Kōno, and Tanaka, with each head handing down the role), and shrine assistants (from the Kawashima family, inherited over generations). The bettō office, until the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, was located at the temple 【Enryaku-ji】’s branch temple, and later at the branch temple of 【Kannen-ji】 called “Rinkaizan Henjō-ji Kongo-in.” According to temple tradition, this bettō establishment was founded in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 5 ({{ill|1194|ja|1194|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 the policy of separating Shinto and Buddhism led to the abolition of the bettō, and the priest became the chief official. In Meiji 5 the title was changed to “Shikikan” (under whom a “Shikashō” was placed), and in Meiji 27 ({{ill|1894|ja|1894|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) it was renamed “Shashii” (with a subordinate “Shashō”). In Shōwa 21 (June {{ill|1946|ja|1946|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) it was finally reorganized into the present system of the chief priest (宮司) with his assistants. Incidentally, since the Meiji period the priests (or chief priests) have at times been men with experience as senior government officials; for example, {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|ja|稲葉正邦|qq=draft|qq=draft}} served from November {{ill|1874|ja|1874|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to May {{ill|1878|ja|1878|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shikikan), then from July {{ill|1879|ja|1879|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to June {{ill|1882|ja|1882|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and again from April {{ill|1882|ja|1882|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to November {{ill|1889|ja|1889|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shikikan), and from August {{ill|1895|ja|1895|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to May {{ill|1897|ja|1897|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shashii). In many cases, men of kazoku (nobility) held the office. === Parishioners (Ujiko) === Below is an outline of the various local parish associations and their approximate present-day areas: * Shinbashi Rozuki-chō Neighborhood Association (covering parts of Shinbashi 4‑chome, 5‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 6‑chome Higashi-chō Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome, 6‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 5・6‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome and 6‑chome) * Shinbashi 7‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 6‑chome and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome) * Shibahama Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome and Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome & Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Neighborhood Association * Shibahama 4‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome and Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Kaigan 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (Kaigan 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Kita Shin Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Miyamotochō Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Naka‑ichi Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 1‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Shiba Daimon Naka‑ni Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 2‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Naka‑3 Sanjichi Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 3‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Katamonzen Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome and Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shiba Park 2‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association (formerly known as Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association, Kin San Shinwa Association, Kin Shi Shinsei Jichikai, Kanesugikawaguchi Neighborhood, and Kanehama Shinboku Association; now parts of Shiba 1‑chome and Shiba 2‑chome) * Shiba Niibori Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba 2‑chome and Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba Zaiōji Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 2‑chome) * A portion of Hokushikoku Neighborhood Association (formerly “Sandai Shikoku Higashi-bu”, now part of Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba 3‑chome Matsumoto Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 3‑chome){{Wayback|url=http://www.geocities.jp/mmyosimoto/ |title=芝松本町 |date=20030628112752}} * Shinmonzen Mutsumi Association (formerly “Shiba Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Sanda 1‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 2‑chome Kita Shinmutsumi Association (formerly “Azabu Kita Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Higashi Azabu 2‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 3‑chome Neighborhood Association (formerly “Shinami 1‑chome”, now parts of Higashi Azabu 3‑chome and Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) * A portion of Shin Niikai (formerly “Shinami 2‑chome”, now part of Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) === Annual Events === ; Main Festival (September 16) : Centered on the festival held on September 16, various rituals including mikoshi processions take place from September 11 to 21. Because these events continue “dara dara” (i.e. dragging on) over a long period, the festival has long been known as the “Dara Dara Festival.” In addition, because ginger is distributed during this period, it is also called the “Ginger Festival” (see the section “Offerings” below). ; Savings Festival (October 17) : In commemoration of the achievements of {{ill|Makino Motonanjirō|ja|牧野元次郎|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (1874–1942), who established a savings bank (the predecessor of the present {{ill|Resona Bank|ja|りそな銀行|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, formerly Asahi Bank and Kyōwa Bank) in the vicinity, a “Savings Mound” (with an inscription by {{ill|Musha Kojii Atsutoku|ja|武者小路実篤|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) was erected on the shrine grounds in Shōwa 32 (1957), and ever since, annual prayers for the protection of savings have been conducted. ; Setsubun Festival (February) : On this day the “Hanchō Festival” is held. This ritual is performed by the “Megumi” fire brigade of Edo town—which administers the shrine’s parish area. It is said that during an incident known as the “Megumi Fight” that took place on the shrine grounds in February of Bunka 2 (1805), the ringing of the hanchō (half bell) led to a great commotion. (The hanchō was once exiled but was later returned to the shrine in the Meiji period.) {| border=1 |- | rowspan=2|January || 1 || New Year’s Festival || rowspan=1|June || 30 || Summer Purification Ceremony |- | 2nd Sunday || Coming-of-Age Festival || rowspan=4|September || 3rd Monday || Respect for the Aged Festival |- | rowspan=3|February || 3 || Setsubun Festival || 11–21 || Main Festival |- | 11 || Foundation Festival || 16 || Ritual of the Main Festival |- | 23 || Tenchō Festival (Mid-Rite) || Autumn Equinox || Autumn Equinox Festival |- | rowspan=2|March || 7 || Harvest Prayer Festival (Grand Festival) || rowspan=3|October || 3rd Monday || Sports Festival |- | Vernal Equinox || Vernal Equinox Festival || rowspan=2|17 || Kaminarai Festival |- | rowspan=2|April || 1 || New Enterprise Prayer Festival || Savings Festival |- | 29 || Shōwa Day Festival || rowspan=2|November || 3 || Culture Day Festival |- | rowspan=2|May || 3 || Constitution Memorial Festival || 23 || Niiname Festival (Grand Festival) |- | 5 || Children’s Festival || rowspan=1|December || 31 || New Year Purification Ceremony |} === Kagura (Sacred Dance) === {{Expand section}} == Auxiliary Shrines == In old times many subsidiary (sessha and massha) shrines were located both within and around the grounds, but presently all have been merged into the main shrine. The following describes the situation before the merger. === Within the Shrine Grounds === Until the fire in January {{ill|1876|ja|1876|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the following subsidiary shrines (with their principal deities) were enshrined on the grounds: ; Sessha * {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine|ja|住吉神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (deities: {{ill|Sumeru no Mikoto|ja|住吉三神|lt=Sumeru deities|lt_ja=表筒男命・中筒男命・底筒男命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) : Formerly known as “Mitarai-sha,” this shrine—located by a pond called Izumigashira—was enshrined as a guardian of the pond. (In the early Meiji period the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Ōwatatsumi no Mikoto|ja|大綿津見命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.) ; Massha * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Kumano Shrine|ja|熊野神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Izanami|ja|伊邪那美命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Suga Shrine|ja|須賀神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|須佐之男命|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt_ja=須佐之男之命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Kotokoronoshi Shrine|ja|事代神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kensoku Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|健速須佐之男命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Hachiman Shrine|ja|八幡神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Asama Shrine|ja|浅間神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|木花咲耶姫命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Ichikishima Shrine|ja|市杵嶋神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Suwa Shrine|ja|諏訪神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Tatemikata-no-Kami|ja|建御名方神|lt=Kenmi-no-Kata|lt_ja=健御名方神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Tenman Shrine|ja|天満神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|Sugawara no Michizane|lt=Sugawara Daijin|lt_ja=菅原大神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Jitsuro Inari Shrine|ja|実禄稲荷社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ho-Shokujin|ja|保食神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Fukushu Inari Shrine|ja|福寿稲荷神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Wakumusubi|ja|ワクムスヒ|lt=Wakumusubi|lt_ja=和加産毘命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * Inari Trio – enshrining {{ill|Ukano Mitama|ja|宇賀魂神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} After 1876, due to mergers and fires (for example, during the Great Kantō Earthquake), in Shōwa 11 ({{ill|1936|ja|1936|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 12 a single subsidiary shrine was rebuilt; with the merger of all the auxiliary shrines, since deities such as {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sukunahikona|ja|少彦名命|1=Sukunabikona|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were enshrined, the shrine came to be regarded as one that confers protection for milestones (such as 60th, 70th, 77th, or 99th birthdays). However, these too were destroyed during the conflagration of the Second World War.For reference, below is the situation of the merged shrines in Shōwa 11 (listing the old auxiliary shrine names, principal deities, and their divine virtues): {| border=0 |- | Izumo Shrine || {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}} || Grain, commerce, trade |- | Mishima Shrine || {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫命|qq=draft|qq=draft}} || Maritime, navigation, seafaring |} === Outside the Shrine Grounds === * Kaida Inari * U spawn Inari (産千代稲荷) * Shiohiki Inari (潮干稲荷) * Chidō Inari (智童稲荷) == Offerings == * Chigibako (木筥) – The chigibako is said either to have originated from using leftover materials (wooden planks called “chigi” that were used to make a rice container) at the time of the shrine’s construction or from the abbreviation of “mochiki” (a vessel for mounded rice cakes). Today, the chigibako—into which beans are placed—may be hung in a room to ward off lightning. * Shiba Shinmei Ginger – At the time the shrine was founded, the surrounding area was known for its flourishing ginger fields. It is said that ginger was offered before the deity; thereafter, consuming the ginger removed from the altar became reputed to prevent colds, and during the annual festival ginger is again distributed. == Cultural Properties == ; Nagasawa Ashisetsu Painted Portrait (人物図): Tangible Cultural Property (painting) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Colored Paper Mount Hakonoyeizu by Tatebe Suso (建部巣兆筆): Tangible Cultural Property (painting) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kagura Mask with “Kagura Mask Catalogue” attached: Tangible Cultural Property (sculpture) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kagura Mask: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (sculpture) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Ashikaga Naoyoshi’s Teaching Document: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Kira Clan Red Seal Document: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Inaha Hanjūrō Chūji Letter: Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Sacred Edict: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Document of the Bettō/Priests: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (ancient document) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Bronze Lantern: Registered Tangible Cultural Property (historical material) in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; The Power Stone of Shiba Daijingu: Tangible Folk Cultural Property designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Hanchō of the Megumi Group: Registered Tangible Folk Cultural Property in Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} == Access == * 5‑minute walk from Hamamatsuchō Station on the {{ill|JR Yamanote Line|ja|山手線|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{Shrine |Name = Shiba Daijingu (芝大神宮) |image = [[File:Shiba-daijingu1.jpg|260px|Shiba Daijingu]]
Worship Hall
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=260|coord={{coord|35|39|27.5|N|139|45|11|E}}}} |Location = 1‑12‑7 Shiba Daimon, Minato, Tokyo {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Latitude = 35|Minutes = 39|Seconds = 27.5 |Longitude = 139|Minutes = 45|Seconds = 11 |Enshrined Deities = {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
{{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Shrine Rank = Former Prefectural Shrine · {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} · Tokyo Ten Shrines |Foundation = {{ill|1005|ja|1005|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2) October 21 |Main Hall = Built in the Shinmei-zukuri style |Alternate Names = Shiba Jinmyōgū · Iikura Jinmyōgū · The Ise of Kanto |Annual Festival = September 16 {{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |Rituals = Hanchō Festival (February 3)
Dara Dara Festival (September 11–21)
Savings Festival (October 17) }} [[File:Shiba-daijingu 01.jpg|thumb|Worship Hall facing east]] '''Shiba Daijingu''' (芝大神宮) is a {{ill|Shinto Shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in 1‑chome of {{ill|Shiba Daimon|ja|芝大門|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in {{ill|Minato|ja|港区 (東京都)|lt=Minato|lt_ja=港区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. At one time it was one of the {{ill|Tokyo Ten Shrines|ja|東京十社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with its former shrine Rank under the modern system being that of a {{ill|Prefectural Shrine|ja|府県社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. == 社名 == Originally, the shrine was simply called “Shinmei” or “Shinmeigū.” Because it was once enshrined in Hibiya-gō in {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it came to be known as “Hibiya Shinmei (Hibiya Shinmeigū)”; and because it was later enshrined at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (later known as Iikura Shō in Musashi Province), it was also called “Iikura Shinmei (Iikura Shinmeigū).” Furthermore, as residents settled in the Shiba area and the town took shape, the name “Shiba Shinmei (Shiba Shinmeigū)” was adopted.{{efn|In Bunsei 10 ({{ill|1827|ja|1827|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), in the “Temple and Shrine Records” section of the “Document of Geographical Survey of Temples and Shrines” (文政寺社町方書上) compiled for the purpose of the “Gofunai Bikō” ({{ill|Gofunai Bikō|ja|御府内備考|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) by the Bakufu ({{ill|Bakufu|ja|Tokugawa shogunate|lt=Bakufu|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the cover was inscribed “Shiba Shinmeisha,” while the document submitted by the shrine to the Bakufu called it “Iikura Shinmeigū.”}} In addition, because the deities of both the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are enshrined here, the shrine played a central role in {{ill|Ise Worship|ja|伊勢信仰|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Kantō region and was respectfully called “The Ise of Kanto.” With the advent of the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and with the approval of the government’s {{ill|Ministry of Religion|ja|教部省|1=Ministry of Religion (Japan)|lt=Ministry of Religion|qq= (Japan)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Daijō-kan Shōin|ja|太政官正院|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tokyo Prefecture|ja|東京府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, from {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 5 ({{ill|August 30 (old calendar)|ja|8月30日 (旧暦)|lt=August 30|lt_ja=8月30日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) ({{ill|1872|ja|1872|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 2|ja|10月2日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) onward the present name “Shiba Daijingu” was adopted. == {{nihongo|Worshipped deities|祭神|Saijin}} == * {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|lt_ja=天照皇大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮内宮|lt=Inner Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=皇大神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * {{ill|Toyouke Ōmikami|ja|トヨウケビメ|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|lt_ja=豊受大御神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the principal deity of the {{ill|Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮外宮|lt=Outer Shrine of Ise Jingu|lt_ja=外宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Unusually for a Tokyo shrine, talismans of Toyouke Ōmikami are also issued. ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|lt_ja=源頼朝公|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** (Side Hall) {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|lt_ja=徳川家康公|qq=draft|qq=draft}} == History == It is said that the shrine traces its origins to a {{ill|Shinmei Shrine|ja|神明社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established at {{ill|Iikura Gochū|ja|飯倉御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – the kitchen ({{ill|Gochū|ja|御厨|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) of {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in Musashi Province – as recorded in the work 『{{ill|Shinpōshō|ja|神鳳鈔|qq=draft|qq=draft}}』. Initially the shrine was enshrined on Iikura-yama (now, {{ill|Shiba Park|ja|芝公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Minato). According to the shrine legend, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Ichijō|ja|一条天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in {{ill|Kankō|ja|寛弘|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1005|ja|1005|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 21|ja|10月21日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on {{ill|September 16 (old calendar)|ja|9月16日 (旧暦)|lt=September 16|lt_ja=9月16日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the inner and outer shrines of Ise were enshrined ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}) and a stone known as “Utodoishi” and a sword—both regarded as sacred treasures—were offered. It is said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft}} twice donated shrine domain lands, in {{ill|Genryaku|ja|元暦|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1185|ja|1185|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 4 ({{ill|1193|ja|1193|qq=draft|qq=draft}}); in the latter instance, over 1,300 kan of land was donated as a shrine domain ({{sfn|江戸名所図会}}). Later in the medieval period the shrine was held in high esteem by the warrior families of eastern Japan. In {{ill|Kenmu|ja|建武|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 4 on {{ill|January 7 (old calendar)|ja|1月7日 (旧暦)|lt=January 7|lt_ja=1月7日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1337|ja|1337|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|February 8|ja|2月8日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the younger brother of {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|ja|足利尊氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, namely {{ill|Ashikaga Naoyoshi|ja|足利直義|lt=Ashikaga Naoyoshi|lt_ja=直義|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, offered a letter of reward in recognition of prayers for military success (a document written by Naoyoshi that is preserved at the shrine). During the 【Sengoku period】, the shrine also received veneration from {{ill|Ota Dokan|ja|太田道灌|lt=Ota Dokan|lt_ja=太田資長（道灌）|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 16 on {{ill|July 24 (old calendar)|ja|7月24日 (旧暦)|lt=July 24|lt_ja=7月24日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1588|ja|1588|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|September 14|ja|9月14日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), an official edict concerning Shibamura was issued by {{ill|Hojo Ujinao|ja|北条氏直|lt=Hojo Ujinao|lt_ja=北条氏直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (this edict is also preserved at the shrine). Furthermore, around {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 18 on {{ill|July 19 (old calendar)|ja|7月19日 (旧暦)|lt=July 19|lt_ja=7月19日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1590|ja|1590|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|August 18|ja|8月18日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|ja|豊臣秀吉|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for military victory when dispatching forces from Edo to pacify the Ou region, and in the same year, on {{ill|August 1 (old calendar)|ja|8月1日 (旧暦)|lt=August 1|lt_ja=8月1日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|August 30|ja|8月30日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|ja|徳川家康|qq=draft|qq=draft}} visited the shrine upon his entry into Edo; then, in the following year on {{ill|November 28 (old calendar)|ja|11月28日 (旧暦)|lt=November 28|lt_ja=11月28日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1592|ja|1592|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|January 12|ja|1月12日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), he donated 15 koku of land in Hibiya of Musashi Province as shrine domain. In {{ill|Keichō|ja|慶長|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 3 (1598) in August, when {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was relocated from the shrine’s former site (Shiba Park), the shrine was moved to its present location (Shiba Daimon, Minato). In the 5th year ({{ill|1600|ja|1600|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|October 7|ja|10月7日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) following the move, Ieyasu himself visited the shrine on his way to the {{ill|Battle of Sekigahara|ja|関ヶ原の戦い|lt=Sekigahara|lt_ja=関ヶ原|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to pray for victory; and during the Siege of Osaka in the 19th to 20th years, as a proxy for the shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|ja|徳川秀忠|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|lt_ja=秀忠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}’s principal wife Oeyo ({{ill|Sūgen-in|ja|崇源院|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), the nurse of {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|ja|徳川家光|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|lt_ja=家光|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kasuga no Tsubone|ja|春日局|qq=draft|qq=draft}} made a shrine visit. Thereafter, under the patronage of successive shōguns and the Bakufu, the construction and repair of the shrine buildings were executed by imperial orders, and various prayer requests were received from the Bakufu (for example, a prayer for safe delivery on the occasion of the birth of the 4th shōgun, {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) – and the shrine was also revered by feudal lords and other regional authorities (for instance, repairs to the shrine buildings were undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the Fukui Domain, and the lord of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|lt=Satsuma Domain Lord|lt_ja=薩摩藩主|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, enshrined the deity in Kagoshima (presently at {{ill|Taga Shrine|ja|多賀神社 (鹿児島市)|lt=Taga Shrine|lt_ja=多賀神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Shimizu-cho, Kagoshima City)).{{efn|Examples include the safe-delivery prayer for the birth of the 4th shōgun {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|ja|徳川家綱|lt=Tokugawa Ietsuna|lt_ja=家綱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and the shrine repairs undertaken by the mother of {{ill|Matsudaira Tadanobu|ja|松平忠直|qq=draft|qq=draft}} of the Echizen Fukui Domain, as well as the enshrinement by the lord of the Satsuma Domain, {{ill|Shimazu Yoshitaka|ja|島津吉貴|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in Kagoshima.}} {{efn|Regarding the above, the following is an excerpt from the “Bunsei Jūnen Shojō” (文政十年書上) that records the shrine’s founding legend for reference: {{Quotation| The origin of enshrining the twin deities at the Great Shrine in Hibiya-gō of Toyoshima District in Musashi Province is said to date from the sixteenth day of September in the second year of Kankō during the reign of Emperor Ichijō. On that day, a sacred token together with a large fang descended upon this place. All the village’s elders, youths, and children gathered, and though they were at first suspicious of the seemingly miraculous descent of this divine token of Shinmei, a little girl inexplicably approached. Her face changed as she hurriedly proclaimed, “I am the divine wind—the deity of both the inner and outer shrines of Ise—and because there is military strife in these eastern lands, I have come down to subdue the armies and mark this place as my dwelling.” Thus, two types of tokens were manifested and promptly shown to you; you must hasten to build a shrine and perform the rites. If you revere me truly, may this place prosper and flourish for all time; I shall also be your guardian deity. Moreover, in Sagami Province there lived a man of the Fujiwara clan bearing the Nishi-Tō name. Invited to serve as head priest, he organized the shrine service. On the twenty-first day of that same month, the sacred rites were performed diligently. The palace, standing facing east before the former horse grounds and extending for several tens of ken, was bordered by rows of trees. In its midst there stood three central torii and two side torii. Notably, one torii was located on the eastern seashore where the tide ebbed; at its base there was a net-like structure. The seashore continued uninterrupted toward the southeast, linking the regions of Anbō and Kazusa. Along the beach, fishermen dwelt and fished. Behind the palace, from the Asabu plateau, a roadway for travelers to the eastern lands was laid out. To the north, in the district of Sakurada, a river flowing there was named Sakuragawa, which eventually merged with a stream that ran by the shrine. Farther northeast, a small stream flowed from behind the palace and ultimately reached the eastern sea. In the vicinity of this river there were abundant rice fields and rustic farmlands, and the lands around the palace were intensively cultivated by many farmers. Some produced confectioneries and were also renowned for growing ginger. Because of the region’s rich harvest of the five grains, the area—since the time the granaries were built—came to be known in local tradition as the “Iikura territory” (and sometimes as Iikura Village). Yet, owing to its humble state, a modest shrine was erected; divine oracles were consulted, and a hereditary priestly family was established to conduct the sacred rites. As years passed, in Jōkyū 4 when General Yoritomo set forth from Nasu-no in Shimotsuke Province, a treasured sword that had been worn became dislodged and sank to the riverbed of the local Utagawa. Despite earnest search and repeated divine consultations, it was never recovered. Meanwhile, near the riverbank, someone proclaimed that a sacred sword—indeed the very one of divine provenance—could be seen gleaming from the turbulent waters. General Yoritomo, upon hearing this, appointed a guide and, accompanied by a retinue, visited the shrine. In due course, he retrieved the sword from the rapids and enshrined it in the treasury of the shrine, so that the divine virtue might be acknowledged. Moreover, a donation of over 1,300 kan of cultivated land was made to the shrine, and in the following year, the roof of the shrine hall was refined and the mansion aligned; henceforth, the local people rejoiced, and the shrine came to be revered as an illustrious emblem of divine favor. |}} }} In the later years of the Edo period, within the urban environs, the shrine—situated on the boundary between the inner city and outlying areas along the {{ill|Tōkaidō|ja|東海道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (with the nearby presence of Kanesugi Bridge) and adjacent to {{ill|Zōjō-ji|ja|増上寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—attracted increasing numbers of worshippers. For travelers leaving Edo, the shrine was a place to pray for a safe journey, while for those entering the city, it offered assurances of safe passage. In addition, although pilgrimage to {{ill|Ise Jingu|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (known as “okage-mairi”) was common in the Edo period, the high cost and long duration of the journey made it difficult for many; as an alternative, many visited this shrine, which enshrines the same deities, right in Edo. As the number of pilgrims grew, a variety of roadside stalls sprang up along the approach – including tea houses, archery stands, blowgun booths, cosmetics stands (known as “hana no tsuyayaya”), sumo rings, conjuring shows, acrobatics, swordsmanship demonstrations, lottery entertainments, and even theaters and other attractions. In particular, the “Taitai Mochi” of Shiba Shinmei became famed as a souvenir. Furthermore, in the Edo period the publisher {{ill|Izumiya Shiheibe|ja|和泉屋市兵衛|qq=draft|qq=draft}} – well known as a wholesaler of popular illustrated books – is said to have opened a shop near the shrine during the {{ill|Tenmei|ja|天明|qq=draft|qq=draft}} period (1781–89). This area also became a focal point for the mass media. It is also recorded that during the early modern period, beginning with a great fire in the Ōei era (1521–27) originating from a nearby village and several subsequent large fires, the shrine was rebuilt time and again. Among the major reconstructions were: * In Meireki 3 ({{ill|1657|ja|1657|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) January, a great fire ({{ill|Meireki Fire|ja|明暦の大火|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) razed the buildings; reconstruction began in Kanbun 1 ({{ill|1661|ja|1661|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) August. * On {{ill|February 16 (old calendar)|ja|2月16日 (旧暦)|lt=February 16|lt_ja=2月16日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hōreki 12 ({{ill|1762|ja|1762|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|March 11|ja|3月11日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}), another great fire occurred; the shrine was rebuilt in Annan 9 ({{ill|1780|ja|1780|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) November. * In Bunka 3 on {{ill|March 4 (old calendar)|ja|3月4日 (旧暦)|lt=March 4|lt_ja=3月4日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1806|ja|1806|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|April 22|ja|4月22日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})), a conflagration occurred; again in Bunsei 7 on {{ill|January 5 (old calendar)|ja|1月5日 (旧暦)|lt=January 5|lt_ja=1月5日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1824|ja|1824|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|February 4|ja|2月4日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})); once more in 【Kaei】 3 on {{ill|February 5 (old calendar)|ja|2月5日 (旧暦)|lt=February 5|lt_ja=2月5日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1850|ja|1850|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|March 18|ja|3月18日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})); and finally, in Ansei 2 on {{ill|October 2 (old calendar)|ja|10月2日 (旧暦)|lt=October 2|lt_ja=10月2日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|1855|ja|1855|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|November 11|ja|11月11日|qq=draft|qq=draft}})) a major earthquake occurred during reconstruction which led to collapse. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 ({{ill|1868|ja|1868|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in October, during the imperial trip of {{ill|Emperor Meiji|ja|明治天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the main shrine building was temporarily used as the palace for ladies-in-waiting; on {{ill|November 8 (old calendar)|ja|11月8日 (旧暦)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the shrine was designated as an {{ill|Associate Imperial Shrine|ja|准勅祭社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in the following year ({{ill|1869|ja|1869|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) during a long spell of rainy weather, on {{ill|July 3 (old calendar)|ja|7月3日 (旧暦)|lt=July 3|lt_ja=7月3日|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, an imperial request was made for prayers to end the rain. However, on {{ill|September 1 (old calendar)|ja|9月1日 (旧暦)|lt=September 1|lt_ja=9月1日|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|1870|ja|1870|qq=draft|qq=draft}} the Associate Imperial Shrine system was abolished, and the shrine became a Prefectural Shrine under Tokyo Prefecture. On January 4, {{ill|1876|ja|1876|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a fire destroyed the building; it was rebuilt in March of the following year ({{ill|1877|ja|1877|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Then in Taishō 12 ({{ill|1923|ja|1923|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 1, the Great Kantō Earthquake caused the structure to collapse and burn. In {{ill|Shōwa|ja|昭和|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 2 ({{ill|1927|ja|1927|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in August the main structures were rebuilt, and in Shōwa 13 ({{ill|1938|ja|1938|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) in December a complete reconstruction was accomplished. However, on May 26, {{ill|1945|ja|1945|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the building was again destroyed by fire during the Tokyo Air Raid at the end of World War II. In the postwar period the shrine joined the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and in Shōwa 22 ({{ill|1947|ja|1947|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on January 13 the main hall was rebuilt; later, in Shōwa 39 ({{ill|1964|ja|1964|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 12 the reconstruction was completed, and on September 16, {{ill|Heisei|ja|平成|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 17 ({{ill|2005|ja|2005|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) during the annual festival a “Shiba Daijingu One-Thousand-Year Festival” was held to celebrate the shrine’s millennium, together with extensive renovations of the administrative office and other structures, forming the present appearance. {{quotation|“'''Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi''' Anko-mochi that has been cherished as a souvenir since the Edo period. It is famously among the offerings of Shiba Shinmei, along with a local folk toy known as the ‘Chikibako’ (a box shaped like a small coin made of wooden planks, arranged in three tiers and bound with straw, on whose surface a wisteria flower is painted in earthen pigment—since the term ‘Chigi’ suggests ‘thousand garments,’ it is said that eating the roasted beans from inside the box will ward off lightning). A paper slip marked “Shiba Miya Taitai Mochi” is also copied.” – Excerpt from Haruharu Shimizu’s _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40), from the section “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library Collection, accessed February 9, 2018.Haruharu Shimizu, _Tokyo Meibutsu Hyakunin Isshu_ (August, Shōwa 40): “Shiba Shinmei’s Taitai Mochi”, National Diet Library, accessed February 9, 2018}} == Rites == === Priestly Office (Shinto Clergy) === Until the Meiji period, the shrine’s affairs were administered by a threefold system consisting of two families of priests (kamiguji) and a group of temple priests (bettō). The bettō was the chief official. When the shrine was founded, Saiyō Katsutoshi was appointed as the priest; thereafter the Saidō family inherited the priesthood. By the late 11th or early 12th century a separate branch was established, and the priestly office was passed down within the two families – the Saidō and the Koizumi. However, during the Bunsei era (1818–1829) no successor emerged from the separate Saidō branch, so a priest was recruited from the Koizumi family of the Inari shrine at Kitashinagawa (present {{ill|Shinagawa Shrine|ja|品川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}); the family name remained Koizumi, and from then on the two families, Saidō and Koizumi, shared the priesthood. Under the priests were officials including the Ōnengui (the heads of the Kaburagi family, inherited over generations), the Neigi (a fixed group of seven – from the families of Moriya, Nakahara, Tada, Masuo, Tamekawa, Kōno, and Tanaka, with each head handing down the role), and shrine assistants (from the Kawashima family, inherited over generations). The bettō office, until the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, was located at the temple 【Enryaku-ji】’s branch temple, and later at the branch temple of 【Kannen-ji】 called “Rinkaizan Henjō-ji Kongo-in.” According to temple tradition, this bettō establishment was founded in {{ill|Kenkyū|ja|建久|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 5 ({{ill|1194|ja|1194|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|1=Meiji era|qq=draft|qq=draft}} 1 the policy of separating Shinto and Buddhism led to the abolition of the bettō, and the priest became the chief official. In Meiji 5 the title was changed to “Shikikan” (under whom a “Shikashō” was placed), and in Meiji 27 ({{ill|1894|ja|1894|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) it was renamed “Shashii” (with a subordinate “Shashō”). In Shōwa 21 (June {{ill|1946|ja|1946|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) it was finally reorganized into the present system of the chief priest (宮司) with his assistants. Incidentally, since the Meiji period the priests (or chief priests) have at times been men with experience as senior government officials; for example, {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|ja|稲葉正邦|qq=draft|qq=draft}} served from November {{ill|1874|ja|1874|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to May {{ill|1878|ja|1878|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shikikan), then from July {{ill|1879|ja|1879|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to June {{ill|1882|ja|1882|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and again from April {{ill|1882|ja|1882|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to November {{ill|1889|ja|1889|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shikikan), and from August {{ill|1895|ja|1895|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to May {{ill|1897|ja|1897|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (as Shashii). In many cases, men of kazoku (nobility) held the office. === Parishioners (Ujiko) === Below is an outline of the various local parish associations and their approximate present-day areas: * Shinbashi Rozuki-chō Neighborhood Association (covering parts of Shinbashi 4‑chome, 5‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 6‑chome Higashi-chō Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome, 6‑chome, and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Shinbashi 5・6‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 5‑chome and 6‑chome) * Shinbashi 7‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Shinbashi 6‑chome and Higashi‑Shinbashi 2‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome) * Shibahama Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 1‑chome and Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome & Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Neighborhood Association * Shibahama 4‑chome Neighborhood Association (parts of Hamamatsuchō 2‑chome and Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Kaigan 1‑chome Neighborhood Association (Kaigan 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Kita Shin Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 1‑chome Miyamotochō Association (a part of Shiba Daimon 1‑chome) * Shiba Daimon 2‑chome Naka‑ichi Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 1‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Shiba Daimon Naka‑ni Neighborhood Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 2‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Naka‑3 Sanjichi Association (formerly “Nakamonzen 3‑chome”, now part of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome) * Katamonzen Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba Daimon 2‑chome and Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shiba Park 2‑chome Neighborhood Association (a portion of Shiba Park 2‑chome) * Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association (formerly known as Shibakanesugi Neighborhood Association, Kin San Shinwa Association, Kin Shi Shinsei Jichikai, Kanesugikawaguchi Neighborhood, and Kanehama Shinboku Association; now parts of Shiba 1‑chome and Shiba 2‑chome) * Shiba Niibori Neighborhood Association (parts of Shiba 2‑chome and Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba Zaiōji Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 2‑chome) * A portion of Hokushikoku Neighborhood Association (formerly “Sandai Shikoku Higashi-bu”, now part of Shiba 3‑chome) * Shiba 3‑chome Matsumoto Neighborhood Association (a part of Shiba 3‑chome){{Wayback|url=http://www.geocities.jp/mmyosimoto/ |title=芝松本町 |date=20030628112752}} * Shinmonzen Mutsumi Association (formerly “Shiba Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Sanda 1‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 2‑chome Kita Shinmutsumi Association (formerly “Azabu Kita Shinmonzen-chō”, now part of Higashi Azabu 2‑chome) * Higashi Azabu 3‑chome Neighborhood Association (formerly “Shinami 1‑chome”, now parts of Higashi Azabu 3‑chome and Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) * A portion of Shin Niikai (formerly “Shinami 2‑chome”, now part of Azabu-Jūban 1‑chome) === Annual Events === ; Main Festival (September 16) : Centered on the festival held on September 16, various rituals including mikoshi processions take place from September 11 to 21. Because these events continue “dara dara” (i.e. dragging on) over a long period, the festival has long been known as the “Dara Dara Festival.” In addition, because ginger is distributed during this period, it is also called the “Ginger Festival” (see the section “Offerings” below). ; Savings Festival (October 17) : In commemoration of the achievements of {{ill|Makino Motonanjirō|ja|牧野元次郎|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (1874–1942), who established a savings bank (the predecessor of the present {{ill|Resona Bank|ja|りそな銀行|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, formerly Asahi Bank and Kyōwa Bank) in the vicinity, a “Savings Mound” (with an inscription by {{ill|Musha Kojii Atsutoku|ja|武者小路実篤|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) was erected on the shrine grounds in Shōwa 32 (1957), and ever since, annual prayers for the protection of savings have been conducted. ; Setsubun Festival (February) : On this day the “Hanchō Festival” is held. This ritual is performed by the “Megumi” fire brigade of Edo town—which administers the shrine’s parish area. It is said that during an incident known as the “Megumi Fight” that took place on the shrine grounds in February of Bunka 2 (1805), the ringing of the hanchō (half bell) led to a great commotion. (The hanchō was once exiled but was later returned to the shrine in the Meiji period.) {| border=1 |- | rowspan=2|January || 1 || New Year’s Festival || rowspan=1|June || 30 || Summer Purification Ceremony |- | 2nd Sunday || Coming-of-Age Festival || rowspan=4|September || 3rd Monday || Respect for the Aged Festival |- | rowspan=3|February || 3 || Setsubun Festival || 11–21 || Main Festival |- | 11 || Foundation Festival || 16 || Ritual of the Main Festival |- | 23 || Tenchō Festival (Mid-Rite) || Autumn Equinox || Autumn Equinox Festival |- | rowspan=2|March || 7 || Harvest Prayer Festival (Grand Festival) || rowspan=3|October || 3rd Monday || Sports Festival |- | Vernal Equinox || Vernal Equinox Festival || rowspan=2|17 || Kaminarai Festival |- | rowspan=2|April || 1 || New Enterprise Prayer Festival || Savings Festival |- | 29 || Shōwa Day Festival || rowspan=2|November || 3 || Culture Day Festival |- | rowspan=2|May || 3 || Constitution Memorial Festival || 23 || Niiname Festival (Grand Festival) |- | 5 || Children’s Festival || rowspan=1|December || 31 || New Year Purification Ceremony |} === Kagura (Sacred Dance) === {{Expand section}} == Auxiliary Shrines == In old times many subsidiary (sessha and massha) shrines were located both within and around the grounds, but presently all have been merged into the main shrine. The following describes the situation before the merger. === Within the Shrine Grounds === Until the fire in January {{ill|1876|ja|1876|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the following subsidiary shrines (with their principal deities) were enshrined on the grounds: ; Sessha * {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine|ja|住吉神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (deities: {{ill|Sumeru no Mikoto|ja|住吉三神|lt=Sumeru deities|lt_ja=表筒男命・中筒男命・底筒男命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) : Formerly known as “Mitarai-sha,” this shrine—located by a pond called Izumigashira—was enshrined as a guardian of the pond. (In the early Meiji period the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Ōwatatsumi no Mikoto|ja|大綿津見命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.) ; Massha * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Kumano Shrine|ja|熊野神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Izanami|ja|伊邪那美命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Suga Shrine|ja|須賀神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|須佐之男命|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt_ja=須佐之男之命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Kotokoronoshi Shrine|ja|事代神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Hikawa Shrine|ja|氷川神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Kensoku Susanoo-no-Mikoto|ja|健速須佐之男命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Hachiman Shrine|ja|八幡神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Asama Shrine|ja|浅間神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|木花咲耶姫命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Ichikishima Shrine|ja|市杵嶋神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ichikishima-hime|ja|市杵島姫命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Suwa Shrine|ja|諏訪神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Tatemikata-no-Kami|ja|建御名方神|lt=Kenmi-no-Kata|lt_ja=健御名方神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Tenman Shrine|ja|天満神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|Sugawara no Michizane|lt=Sugawara Daijin|lt_ja=菅原大神|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Jitsuro Inari Shrine|ja|実禄稲荷社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Ho-Shokujin|ja|保食神|1=Ukemochi|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * {{ill|Fukushu Inari Shrine|ja|福寿稲荷神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Wakumusubi|ja|ワクムスヒ|lt=Wakumusubi|lt_ja=和加産毘命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) * Inari Trio – enshrining {{ill|Ukano Mitama|ja|宇賀魂神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} After 1876, due to mergers and fires (for example, during the Great Kantō Earthquake), in Shōwa 11 ({{ill|1936|ja|1936|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) on September 12 a single subsidiary shrine was rebuilt; with the merger of all the auxiliary shrines, since deities such as {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sukunahikona|ja|少彦名命|1=Sukunabikona|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were enshrined, the shrine came to be regarded as one that confers protection for milestones (such as 60th, 70th, 77th, or 99th birthdays). However, these too were destroyed during the conflagration of the Second World War.For reference, below is the situation of the merged shrines in Shōwa 11 (listing the old auxiliary shrine names, principal deities, and their divine virtues): {| border=0 |- | Izumo Shrine || {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|qq=draft|qq=draft}} || Grain, commerce, trade |- | Mishima Shrine || (智童稲荷) == Offerings == * Chigibako (木筥) – The chigibako is said either to have originated from using leftover materials (wooden planks called “chigi” that were used to make a rice container) at the time of the shrine’s construction or from the abbreviation of “mochiki” (a vessel for mounded rice cakes). Today, the chigibako—into which beans are placed—may be hung in a room to ward off lightning. * Shiba Shinmei Ginger – At the time the shrine was founded, the surrounding area was known for its flourishing ginger fields. It is said that ginger was offered before the deity; thereafter, consuming the ginger removed from the altar became reputed to prevent colds, and during the annual festival ginger is again distributed. == Cultural Properties == ; Nagasawa Ashisetsu Painted Portrait (人物図): Tangible Cultural Property (painting) designated by Minato Ward {{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; Colored Paper Mount Hakonoyeizu {{神社 |名称 = 芝大神宮 |画像 = [[File:Shiba-daijingu1.jpg|260px|芝大神宮]]
拝殿
{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=260|coord={{coord|35|39|27.5|N|139|45|11|E}}}} |所在地 = 東京都港区芝大門一丁目12番7号{{sfn|東京都神社庁}} | 緯度度 = 35|緯度分 = 39|緯度秒 = 27.5 | 経度度 = 139|経度分 = 45|経度秒 = 11 |祭神 = [[天照大神|天照皇大御神]]
[[トヨウケビメ|豊受大御神]]{{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |社格 = 旧府社・准勅祭社・東京十社 |創建 = [[1005年]]（[[寛弘]]2年）10月21日 |本殿 = 神明造 |別名 = 芝神明宮・飯倉神明宮・関東のお伊勢様 |例祭 = 9月16日{{sfn|東京都神社庁}} |神事 = 半鐘祭（2月3日）
だらだら祭り（9月11-21日）
貯金祭（10月17日） }} [[File:Shiba-daijingu 01.jpg|thumb|東を向いて建つ拝殿]] '''芝大神宮'''（しばだいじんぐう）は、[[東京都]][[港区 (東京都)|港区]][[芝大門]]一丁目に鎮座する[[神社]]である。一時期[[准勅祭社]]とされた[[東京十社]]の1社で、[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[府県社|府社]]。 == 社名 == もともとは、単に「神明」あるいは「神明宮」と称していたが、[[武蔵国]]日比谷郷に鎮座していたことから「日比谷神明（日比谷神明宮）」と、また[[飯倉御厨]]（後の武蔵国飯倉庄）に鎮座していたことから、「飯倉神明（飯倉神明宮）」と、さらに芝の地に住民が居留して町の様相を呈するに及び「芝神明（芝神明宮）」とも称されるに至った{{efn|文政10年（[[1827年]]）の[[江戸幕府|幕府]]による「[[御府内備考]]」編纂のための史料たる「[[地誌御調書上帳]]」（文政寺社町方書上）の「寺社書上」では、表紙に「芝神明社」と書かれ、当神社から幕府に提出した書面では「飯倉神明宮」と称していた。}}。また別に、[[伊勢神宮]]の内外両宮の祭神を祀ることから、関東における[[伊勢信仰]]の中心的な役割を担い、「関東のお伊勢様」とも尊称された。[[明治維新]]にあたり、政府の[[教部省]]、[[正院|太政官正院]]並びに[[東京府]]の許可のもと、[[明治]]5年[[8月30日 (旧暦)|8月30日]]（[[1872年]][[10月2日]]）より、現今の神社名である「芝大神宮」を称す。 == 祭神 == * [[天照大神|天照皇大御神]] - [[皇大神宮|伊勢神宮内宮]]の主祭神である。 * [[トヨウケビメ|豊受大御神]] - [[外宮|伊勢神宮外宮]]の主祭神である。東京都内では珍しく「豊受大御神」の神札も授与している。 ** （相殿）[[源頼朝|源頼朝公]] ** （相殿）[[徳川家康|徳川家康公]] == 歴史 == 武蔵国に置かれた伊勢神宮の[[御厨]]である「飯倉御厨」（『[[神鳳鈔]]』）に創祀された[[神明社]]に起源を持つとされ、当初は飯倉山（現港区[[芝公園]]）に鎮座していた。社伝によれば、[[一条天皇]]の御代、[[寛弘]]2年[[9月16日 (旧暦)|9月16日]]（[[1005年]][[10月21日]]）、伊勢の内外両宮を[[勧請]]して創建し{{sfn|江戸名所図会}}、[[日向国]]鵜戸郡から得た「鵜戸石」と剣を神宝として奉納したといい、[[源頼朝]]は[[元暦]]元年（[[1185年]]）と[[建久]]4年（[[1193年]]）の2度に亘って[[神領]]を寄進し、特に後者においては自ら社参の上1300余貫の地を[[神田]]として寄進したという{{sfn|江戸名所図会}}。その後中世には東国武家から厚く崇敬され、[[建武 (日本)|建武]]4年[[1月7日 (旧暦)|1月7日]]（[[1337年]][[2月8日]]）には、[[足利尊氏]]の実弟[[足利直義|直義]]が戦捷祈願に対する報賽の書状を奉納したほか（神社所蔵の伝直義執筆書状）、[[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]には[[太田道灌|太田資長（道灌）]]の崇敬を受け、[[天正]]16年[[7月24日 (旧暦)|7月24日]]（[[1588年]][[9月14日]]）には、[[北条氏直]]による柴村に対しての制札が発布された（この制札も神社所蔵）。また、[[豊臣秀吉]]も天正18年[[7月19日 (旧暦)|7月19日]]（[[1590年]][[8月18日]]）あたりに、奥羽平定のために江戸を進発するに際して戦捷を祈願し、[[徳川家康]]も同年[[8月1日 (旧暦)|8月1日]]（[[8月30日]]）、江戸入府に際して社参、翌19年[[11月28日 (旧暦)|11月28日]]（[[1592年]][[1月12日]]）、武蔵国日比谷郷に社領15石を寄進した。[[慶長]]3年（1598年）8月、[[増上寺]]が当神社の旧鎮座地（芝公園）へ移転することとなったため、現在地（港区芝大門）へ奉遷し、翌々5年[[9月1日 (旧暦)|9月1日]]（[[1600年]][[10月7日]]）、家康は[[関ヶ原の戦い|関ヶ原]]出陣に際し、社参して戦捷祈願をし、同19年から20年にかけての[[大坂の陣]]では、徳川方の戦捷祈願をするべく、将軍[[徳川秀忠|秀忠]]の正室お江与の方（[[崇源院]]）の代参として、[[徳川家光|家光]]の乳母である[[春日局]]が社参をしている。以後、歴代将軍家・幕府の庇護を受け、社殿の造営・修復等は幕命により執行するとともに、幕府より種々の祈祷依頼があり{{efn|4代将軍[[徳川家綱|家綱]]誕生に際しての安産祈願等の例がある。}}、大名による参詣等諸侯からも崇敬を受けた{{efn|[[福井藩|越前福井藩主]][[松平忠直]]母清凉院による社殿修復等。また、[[薩摩藩|薩摩藩主]][[島津吉貴]]は、[[鹿児島]]の地に当神社を勧請した（現[[鹿児島市]]清水町鎮座の[[多賀神社 (鹿児島市)|多賀神社]]）。}} {{efn|以上に関し、前掲「文政十年書上」に載せる由緒を参考までに引用する。 {{Quotation| 武蔵国豊嶋郡日比谷郷に両宮太神宮を勧請奉（たてまつ）る由来は、一条院御宇（ぎょう）寛弘二巳年（みのとし）九月十六日にあたりて、御神幣（ごしんぺい）並（ならびに）大牙（たいが）一枚此地（このち）に降り玉ふ（給う）、村中の老少男女集まりて、これいかさまにも神明のあまくた（天降）り玉ふへ（べ）きしるしなるへ（べ）しと、あや（怪）しみ奉（たてまつ）る所に、いつ（ず）くともなく幼女壱人その所にあゆ（歩）み来たり、顔色変し（じ）て口はし（走）りていわく、我ハこれ神風や、伊勢の内外の両宮の神也、これより東国にあたりて軍（いくさ）の事あるゆゑに、常陸国鹿嶋の地に降臨し、その軍兵を退治し、ほと（ど）なく帰座の路におよぶ、我この所に跡をとゝ（ど）めんとおほしめす（思し召す）なり、此故（このゆえ）に二種のしるし（璽）をあらわ（顕）して、先（まず）汝等（なんじら）に示す、はや（早）く宮社を営みをさめ（修め）祭るべし、いかにもとうとみ（尊み）敬はば（うやまわば）、末の世までも此所（このところ）栄へ（さかえ）賑ひてめてたかるへし（目出たかるべし）、我又守りの神とならん、相模国の内に藤原姓西東氏のもの（者）あらん、是をまね（招）きて神職の長となし宮仕へ（みやづかえ）をさせよとて、神明あか（上）らせ玉へハ（ば）、少女あとかた（跡形）なくう（失）せにけり、村中このきとく（奇特）によりて、うち置かたく（打ち置き難く）、小宮を造りて御神幣と大牙を宮にをさめ奉り、西東氏の人を尋ねしかハ、相州足柄の内に西東氏の人あり、御託宣にまか（任）せてまねき寄せ家をつく（造）りて神職をつかさと（司）らしめ、同月廿一日ニ（に）神事をおこなひ（行ない）勤めしとそ（ぞ）、 その宮殿の在（あり）さまハ、東にむか（向）ひ鎮座有（あり）て、前なる馬場先、数十間にして、樹木並びに生（な）して、其中間中間に三の鳥居、二の鳥居あり、就中（なかんずく）、一の鳥居ハ東の海辺にありて汐のさし引（差し引き）、鳥居の元（もと）にいた（至）りて、網干あり、此海つら（面）東南につつき（続き）て向ふハ安房・上総隔（へだたり）なし、浜つつきに海人住て漁いとま（暇）あらず、後ハ阿佐布（麻布）の台よりして東国往来の道路につつ（続）けり、北ハ桜田郷の地にして其川の流れを桜川と号して、末ハ社辺に流れ来れり、夫（それ）より東北にあたりて、わづか（僅か）なる川あり、此河上ハ宮殿の後より流て末ハ東の海へ流れり、此川のあたりは深田多くして田舎あり、宮殿のめぐり（廻り）田畑にて農民数多耕作をなす、或ハ菓を作り、又生姜を作ることに優れて、五穀豊穣の地たるによりて、往昔穀倉の建し時より称したる地名残りて民俗飯倉領と号＜す＞、また、飯倉村とも称しならハせり（倣わせり）、然共（しかれども）、質素の時なる故、讒（わずか）の神祠を営＜み＞、神託にまかセ（せ）て、神職一家を立て神事祭礼と（執）り行ひて、数年の星霜を経、後鳥羽院御宇建久四年壬丑年、右大将頼朝卿下野国那須野に発向し玉ふ時、当地の宇多川に[只今、宇田川町往還ニ有之候（これありそうろう）、桜川の流末、大下水の流にても可有之哉（これあるべきや）に候得共（そうらえども）、聢ト（しかと）難定候（さだめがたくそうろう）]至りて帯（たい）し玉へる御太刀ぬ（抜）けて水底に沈ミ（み）ける、水練のもの（者）をめ（召）して、さがしもとめ（探し求め）さするに、さらになし、ここにかたハら（傍ら）に人ありて申すよふ（様）、此川上に神明の宮ところ（宮所）おハ（わ）します、そのうしろ（後ろ）のかた（方）より瀬ありて水みなぎ（漲）る水底に物ありて光はな（放）つ、是尋ね玉ふ所の御剣なるへしと申＜す＞、右大将きこし召（聞し召し）、彼男を案内者として神明に御参詣ありて、やがてうしろの瀬にして、太刀をもとめ得（え）玉ひ、直ニ神明の御宝殿におさめ玉ひ、御神徳を感し（じ）たまひ、此所におゐて千三百貫の菜地を御寄附あり、其翌年より社殿甍を琢（みが）き、屋宮軒をならへ（べ）神前の警固怠らす（ず）日にま（増）し、繁栄斜ならす（ず）所の民俗悦（よろこび）の眉をひら（開）けり、神領菜地いよいよ豊饒なる神徳のいちしるしき（著しき）を尊称し、飯倉神田と号し、ますます神威、盛にして当国近在の民俗にいたる迄尊敬かきり（限り）なし、ことに当地社人数多有之故（これあるがゆえ）、毎年正月にハ多摩川入間川をさか（境）へ、国家安全の祈念おこたらす（怠らず）、神事祭礼厳重たり、其後、建武年中、'''尊氏公[1]'''よりも判物を給り、弥以（いよいよもって）国家の祈念怠る事なく、当社の神徳他国よりも尊敬あけて（挙げて）かそふ（数う）べからず、然し処に長禄年中、太田'''左衛門佐[2]'''持資入道道灌、豊嶋郡荏土（江戸）の地に始て城を築て居城の地となれり、其後、北条早雲関東を手入（手に入れ）、相州小田原に居城せられ、関東の神社仏閣庄園をお（落）とせし時より当社の領地も削られ、衰微に及へ（べ）り、此時社人等多く退散して玉川（多摩川）入間川に出＜て＞執行し、国家の祈念退転に及へり、然れと（ど）も御鎮座所ハ昔にかはらず（変わらず）事足る侭に古きを追ふの神事祭礼怠る事なく、年を経しに江城北条家に属し'''遠山左衛門[3]'''に至＜る＞迄居城ありけれとも、戦場止時（やむとき）なきころ（頃）なれハ（ば）、聊（いささかも）城主よりの祈祷書通までにて宮殿にも纔（わずか）の経営たりしに、天正年中、家康公関東御領地の時に至り始めて御入国の時、当宮へ御参詣有て鎮座由来、御尋（おたずね）ありしに前段の縁起等委（くわし）く言上せしかハ（ば）、旧地の神域御尊敬の余り飯倉におゐて神明領御寄附ありて、其以後関ケ原御出陣の節も御参詣あつて御願望あり、程なく御開運ニて当地御在城の地に定めさセ給ひ、当地へも時々の御祈祷怠りなく、御尊敬ましまし、今におゐて天下泰平国家安穏御祈祷怠慢なく丹誠を抽むで（ぬきんで）神徳いよいよ盛なり、敬白 }} ::[1] 「尊氏」は過誤で、正しくは「直義」。 ::[2] 「左衛門佐」は過誤で、正しくは「左衛門大夫」。 ::[3] 遠山左衛門尉は江戸城代[[遠山直景|遠山丹波守直景]]か。}}。 また市井においては、[[東海道]]沿線で江戸市中と市外の境界線上（近くに金杉橋あり）に鎮座し、増上寺も隣接することから、江戸時代に入って参詣者が増え、江戸から出府する旅人にとっては道中無事を、入府する旅人にとっては道中無事の報賽をといった祈願が行われた。さらに江戸時代には[[お蔭参り]]といわれる伊勢神宮への参拝が数多く見受けられるが、高額な旅費と長期間の旅程を要し、容易に行うことは難しかったため、代わりに伊勢神宮の祭神を祀り江戸市中に鎮座する当神社への参詣者が増えていったと考えられる。参詣者が増えれば、それを当て込んで参道に数々の出店が見られるようになり、茶屋、揚弓場、吹き矢、花の露屋（化粧品）、角力、手妻（手品）、軽業、剣術、富籤興行、[[岡場所]]・[[陰間]]などの風俗店や、芝居などの見世物小屋で賑わい、特に芝神明の'''太々餅'''は土産物として評判を呼び、名物となった。更に、江戸で出版された娯楽絵本の版元で、[[地本問屋]]として名を馳せた[[和泉屋市兵衛]]が[[天明|天明頃]]（1781-89年）には当神社近隣に店を構えていたといわれ、この界隈はマスコミの拠点にもなっていた。なお、[[大永|大永年間]]（1521-27年）に近村から出火し、大風に煽られた火災によって類焼したのを始めとして、近世にはしばしば大火に見舞われ、その度に再建されている{{efn|主なものを掲げると、 * [[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）1月の[[明暦の大火|大火]]により類焼。[[寛文]]元年（[[1661年]]）8月再建。 * [[宝暦]]12年[[2月16日 (旧暦)|2月16日]]（[[1762年]][[3月11日]]）、大火により類焼。[[安永]]9年（[[1780年]]）11月再建。 * [[文化 (元号)|文化]]3年[[3月4日 (旧暦)|3月4日]]（[[1806年]][[4月22日]]）、類焼。[[文政]]7年[[1月5日 (旧暦)|1月5日]]（[[1824年]][[2月4日]]）、類焼。[[嘉永]]3年[[2月5日 (旧暦)|2月5日]]（[[1850年]][[3月18日]]）、類焼。[[安政]]2年[[10月2日 (旧暦)|10月2日]]（[[1855年]][[11月11日]]）の[[安政の大地震|大地震]]により、再建半ばで再度倒壊。}}。 [[明治]]元年（[[1868年]]）10月、[[明治天皇]]東幸の際、本社を内侍所として小休し、同年[[11月8日 (旧暦)|11月8日]]（[[1868年]][[12月21日]]）、[[准勅祭社]]に指定され、翌2年（[[1869年]]）の長雨に際しては[[7月3日 (旧暦)|7月3日]]（[[8月10日]]）に朝廷より止雨祈祷の依頼があるなど厚遇されたが、明治3年[[9月1日 (旧暦)|9月1日]]（[[1870年]][[9月25日]]）、准勅祭社制度の廃止に伴い、東京府の[[府社]]となった。明治9年（[[1876年]]）1月4日、火災により焼失したため、翌10年（[[1877年]]）3月に再建、[[大正]]12年（[[1923年]]）9月1日の[[関東大震災]]により倒壊延焼したため、[[昭和]]2年（[[1927年]]）8月、本殿等主要建造物を再建し、同13年（[[1938年]]）12月には完全再建されたが、同20年（[[1945年]]）5月26日に[[東京大空襲]]により焼失して終戦を迎えた。戦後は[[神社本庁]]に参加し、昭和22年（[[1947年]]）1月13日に本殿再建、同39年（[[1964年]]）9月12日には本殿再造営が完工し、[[平成]]17年（[[2005年]]）9月16日の例祭では、鎮座1000年を祝う「芝大神宮壱千年祭」を斎行し、併せて社務所等の改築を執り行い、現在の景観となる。 {{quotation|「'''芝神明（芝大神宮）の太々餅'''」 江戸時代から土産物として親しまれたあんころ餅。芝神明の授与品として著名な、郷土玩具の千木筥（経木で作った小判型の曲物（箱）。三つ重ねにして藁で結ばれ、表面には泥絵具で 藤の花が描かれている。千木が千着に通じることから女性の衣服が増えると、箱の中の煎り豆を食べると雷除けになるとも伝えられる）と生姜（祭礼の生姜祭りは、風邪除けで知らる）の絵あり。「芝宮太々餅」と記された紙片が書き写されている。|清水晴風著『東京名物百人一首』明治40年8月「芝神明（芝大神宮）の太々餅」より抜粋清水晴風著『東京名物百人一首』明治40年8月「芝神明（芝大神宮）の太々餅」国立国会図書館蔵書、2018年2月9日閲覧}} == 祭祀 == === 神職 === 明治までは神主家2家と[[別当|別当職]]（僧侶）が三頭体制で社務を執行し、別当が首座とされていた。神主職は創祀にあたって西東（さいとう）勝時が神職とされて以来、西東家が世襲し、11世紀末あるいは12世紀初頭に別家を立てて、2家の西東家にて継承して来たというが、文政年間（1818-1829年）に別家の西東家に後継者が出なかったため、北品川稲荷（現[[品川神社]]）の神主小泉家より迎え、家名小泉をそのままとして以降、西東・小泉の2家となった。神主の下には、大禰宜（鏑木家当主代々継承）・禰宜（定員七名。守屋、中原、多田、増尾、為川、河野、田中の七家があり、各当主が代々禰宜を継承）・社地役人（川嶋家代々当主継承）がいた。また別当職は、[[延暦寺|比叡山延暦寺]]の末寺、また[[寛永寺|東叡山寛永寺]]の末寺であった'''臨海山遍照寺金剛院'''で、寺伝によれば建久5年（[[1194年]]）に芝海辺あたりに開基されたという。 明治元年、[[神仏分離|神仏分離政策]]により別当が廃され、神主が首座とされたが、その名称は同5年に「祠官」（祠官の下に「祠掌」が置かれた）、同27年（[[1894年]]）には「社司」（社司の下に「社掌」）に、さらに昭和21年（[[1946年]]）6月には、現行の宮司（宮司の下に禰宜）と変遷した。ちなみに明治以降の神主（宮司）は、明治7年（[[1874年]]）11月から同11年（[[1878年]]）5月までの[[稲葉正邦]]（祠官）、11年7月から翌12年（[[1879年]]）6月までと同15年（[[1882年]]）4月から22年（[[1889年]]）11月まで（祠官）、同28年（[[1895年]]）8月から30年（[[1897年]]）5月まで（社司）の[[諏訪忠誠]]のように、幕末の[[老中]]経験者が勤めたことはあるものの、概ね[[子爵]]が就任した。 9月16日の例祭を中心に、9月11日から21日まで、神輿渡御などの各種神事が行われるが、それらが長期間「だらだら」と続くために、古来より「だらだら祭り」とも言われている。また期間中に[[生姜]]を授与しているところから、別名「生姜祭り」とも称した（後述[[#授与品|「授与品」の節]]も参照）。 ; 貯金祭（10月17日） : 近隣地に現在の[[りそな銀行]]（旧[[あさひ銀行]]・旧[[協和銀行]]）につながる[[不動貯金銀行]]を設立し、貯金王と称された[[牧野元次郎]]（[[1874年]]-[[1942年]]）の偉業を称え、昭和32年（[[1957年]]）、当時の関係者により境内に貯金塚（碑文は、[[武者小路実篤]]筆）が建立され、以後、毎年、貯蓄・貯金の加護祈請を執行している。 ; 節分祭（2月） : 当日には、「[[半鐘]]祭」が執行される。これは、当神社の氏子域を管轄する江戸町火消しの「め組」衆が参詣し執行している。当神社は、文化2年（1805年）2月に境内で起こった「[[め組の喧嘩]]」の舞台であり、この半鐘を鳴らしたため騒ぎが大きくなったといわれる。半鐘は[[遠島]]処分になり明治時代になって当神社に戻ってきた。 {| border=1 |- | rowspan=2|1月||1日||元旦祭|| rowspan=1|6月||30日||大祓式（夏越） |- |第2日曜日||成人祭|| rowspan=4|9月||第三月曜日||敬老祭 |- | rowspan=3|2月||3日||節分祭||11～21日||例大祭 |- |11日||紀元祭||16日||例大祭祭儀 |- |23日||天長節（中祭）||秋分の日||秋分祭 |- | rowspan=2|3月||7日||祈年祭（大祭）|| rowspan=3|10月||第3月曜日||体育祭 |- |春分の日||春分祭|| rowspan=2|17日||神嘗祭 |- | rowspan=2|4月||1日||新事業祈願祭||貯金祭 |- |29日||昭和の日祭|| rowspan=2|11月||3日||文化の日祭 |- | rowspan=2|5月||3日||憲法記念祭||23日||新嘗祭（大祭） |- |5日||こども祭|| rowspan=1|12月||31日||大祓式（年越） |} === 神楽 === {{節スタブ}} == 摂末社 == 古くは境内外に多くの摂末社を所管していたが、現在は全て本殿に合祀されている。以下合祀以前の概況を述べる。 === 境内社 === 明治9年（1876年）1月の火災により焼失するまでの境内社に下記の摂末社（主祭神）が鎮座していた。 ; 摂社 * 住吉神社（[[住吉三神|表筒男命・中筒男命・底筒男命]]） *: 古くは御手洗社と称し、戦前まで境内にあった泉頭という池泉の守護神として住吉三柱神を祀り、摂社としたものである（明治初期には、[[オオワタツミ|大綿津見命]]に祭神が変更された）。[[寛永]]10年（[[1633年]]）3月、3代将軍家光が鷹狩りに出向いた時、目にゴミが入って難渋していたところ、この池泉の水で目を洗うとたちどころに快癒したため、感じ入った家光は当神社への尊崇の念を篤くし、老朽化した社殿等の造営に着手したといい、一方、その評判を聞きつけた江戸市民も池泉に参詣して眼病快癒を祈請するようになって以来、眼病平癒に霊験がある神とされたという。 ; 末社 * 春日神社（[[天児屋根命]]） * 熊野神社（[[伊邪那美命]]） * 須賀神社（[[須佐之男命|須佐之男之命]]） * 事代神社（[[事代主命]]） * 氷川神社（健速須佐之男命） * 八幡神社（[[応神天皇]]） * 浅間神社（[[木花咲耶姫命]]） * 市杵嶋神社（[[市杵島姫命]]） * 諏訪神社（[[建御名方神|健御名方神]]） * 天満神社（[[菅原道真|菅原大神]]） * 淡島神社（[[少彦名神|少名彦名神]]） * 宝禄稲荷神社（[[保食神]]） * 福寿稲荷神社（[[ワクムスヒ|和加産毘命]]） * 稲荷社三社（[[ウカノミタマ|宇賀魂神]]） 明治9年以後、合祀が行われたり、[[関東大震災]]などにより焼失したため、昭和11年（[[1936年]]）9月12日に改めて末社1社を再建し、全末社を合祀することとなり、[[オオクニヌシ|大国主命]]、少彦名命、事代主命が祀られていたため、算賀（還暦・古稀・喜寿・米寿など）加護の社とされたが、これも[[第二次世界大戦]]の戦火で焼失した参考までに昭和11年の合祀状況を示す（旧末社名、主祭神、神徳の順）。 {{-}} == 授与品 == * 千木筥（ちぎばこ） - 現在は千木が「千着」に通じることから、女性の衣服が増えるとして、入学祝い・成人祝い・就職祝い・結婚祝い・出産祝い等の贈り物として受ける傾向があるが、神社建立の際の余材である[[千木]]を用いて米櫃を作ったことに起源を持つとか、餅を盛った器（餅器「もちき」）の「も」を略して千器といったとかの諸説がある{{efn|『社記』に、当地は[[宣化天皇]]の御宇に[[屯倉]]が設けられ、その穀倉があったことから土民が穀類の容器を製作するようになり、「千器（ちぎ）はいにしへ藤蔓にて編み器となし餅を盛るによつて飯器（もちき）の上略なり」と記している。}}。また千木筥の中には豆が入っており、部屋に吊るしておくと、[[雷]]除けになるともいう。 * 芝神明生姜 - 当神社創建の時代、周辺には生姜畑が繁茂していたため、これを神前に供えたといい、その撤下を食すと風邪に罹りにくくなるとの評判が生じ、爾来、例祭期間中に生姜を授与するようになったという。 == 文化財 == ; 長沢芦雪筆人物図: 港区指定有形文化財（絵画）{{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; 紙本着色箱根詣図 建部巣兆筆: 港区指定有形民俗文化財{{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} ; め組の半鐘: 港区登録有形民俗文化財{{sfn|港区立郷土歴史館}} == アクセス == * [[東日本旅客鉄道|JR]][[山手線]]・[[京浜東北線]][[浜松町駅]]　徒歩5分 * [[東京都交通局|都営]][[都営地下鉄浅草線|浅草線]]・[[都営地下鉄大江戸線|大江戸線]][[大門駅 (東京都)|大門駅]]　徒歩1分 *
